disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Teaches public NIST SP 800-207 zero-trust concepts; not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by NIST or any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

choices: It's fine — internal users are vetted employees
It's implicit trust based on network location; zero trust requires verifying identity, device health, and context for every access request regardless of location
The VPN needs a bigger license
Internal networks are always safe
scenarios.hint: What is the VPN actually verifying — and what is it assuming?
scenarios.prompt: What is the zero-trust critique of this architecture?
scenarios.situation: The company VPN grants full internal network access to anyone with valid credentials. 'Once you're on the VPN, you're trusted,' the architect says.
scenarios.title: Trusted because VPN
scenarios.why: A VPN authenticates the connection, then extends implicit trust to everything inside — the exact model zero trust rejects. Compromised credentials or an infected laptop get the whole network. Zero trust replaces 'trusted network location' with per-request verification: who, what device, what health, what context — every time.

choices: The firewall — it sees all traffic
The policy engine (decides) and policy administrator (enforces via policy enforcement points) — every access decision flows through them
The SIEM — it correlates everything
The VPN concentrator
scenarios.hint: In a zero-trust model, what component actually says 'yes' or 'no' to an access request?
scenarios.prompt: Per NIST SP 800-207's logical architecture, which components make and enforce access decisions?
scenarios.situation: Your team is mapping the current architecture to NIST SP 800-207's logical components.
scenarios.title: Who decides?
scenarios.why: SP 800-207 centers on the policy engine (evaluates trust and makes the grant/deny decision) and the policy administrator (establishes the communication path), acting through policy enforcement points. Naming these components forces the design question: where in YOUR architecture does the per-request decision actually happen? If the answer is 'nowhere, the firewall did it at connect time,' you're not there yet.

choices: Zero trust means no perimeter at all — remove the firewalls
Zero trust doesn't abolish perimeters; it makes them granular and identity-centric — micro-perimeters around resources with per-request verification
Keep the single perimeter but buy a better firewall
Perimeters are a compliance checkbox only
scenarios.hint: Does 'never trust the network' mean the network has no boundaries, or that the boundaries moved?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct understanding?
scenarios.situation: An executive heard 'zero trust eliminates the perimeter' and proposes removing the edge firewalls.
scenarios.title: Killing the perimeter
scenarios.why: Zero trust shrinks and multiplies the perimeter — down to individual resources and sessions — rather than eliminating it. The big flat 'inside' is what dies. Micro-perimeters (host firewalls, service mesh policies, identity-aware proxies) enforce per-request decisions close to the resource. Removing edge controls without replacing them with granular enforcement is just removing security.

choices: Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorize every request with identity, device posture, and context — no standing trust from the network
Trust but verify: allow first, audit later
Verify once at login, then trust the session indefinitely
Only verify external users; employees are trusted
scenarios.hint: Which word in 'never trust, always verify' do most implementations quietly drop?
scenarios.prompt: What does 'verify explicitly' require in practice?
scenarios.situation: A vendor claims their product is 'zero trust' because it has MFA at login.
scenarios.title: MFA is not zero trust
scenarios.why: MFA at login is one verification of one factor at one moment. 'Verify explicitly' (an SP 800-207 tenet) means using all available data — identity, device health, location, behavior, resource sensitivity — to authorize each access decision, continuously. A product with login MFA and then implicit trust is a VPN with better marketing.

choices: It's a product you buy and deploy
It's an architectural approach and ongoing discipline — products can support it, but no single purchase 'achieves' zero trust
It's a compliance certification
It's only for cloud companies
scenarios.hint: What happens to 'zero trust' the day after the product is installed, when new apps and users arrive?
scenarios.prompt: A vendor promises 'complete zero trust in 30 days.' What is the honest response?
scenarios.situation: Procurement is excited about a vendor's zero-trust-in-a-box pitch.
scenarios.title: Zero trust in a box
scenarios.why: Zero trust is a set of principles applied across identity, devices, networks, apps, and data — an ongoing program, not a SKU. Products can provide enforcement points, identity services, or microsegmentation, but the architecture, policies, and governance are the organization's work. 'In a box' promises confuse buying tools with doing the discipline.

choices: Nothing — breaches are inevitable, accept them
Assume breach: design so compromise of one segment doesn't mean compromise of all — containment, monitoring, and rapid response are architectural requirements
Assume breach means the SOC failed
It only applies to nation-state threats
scenarios.hint: If you assume the attacker is already inside, what do you build differently?
scenarios.prompt: What does the 'assume breach' tenet change?
scenarios.situation: Your CISO asks what 'assume breach' (SP 800-207) means for the network design you're proposing.
scenarios.title: Designing for the breach
scenarios.why: Assume breach converts 'keep them out' into 'limit what they can do when they're in': segmentation contains lateral movement, monitoring detects internal malicious behavior, and least privilege shrinks blast radius. It's not defeatism — it's engineering for the failure mode every major breach demonstrated. The flat trusted LAN is the artifact of the old assumption.

scenarios.title: The VPN is not a moat
scenarios.situation: A company routes all remote access through a VPN and treats everything inside the corporate network as trusted. An attacker phishes one employee's VPN credentials and moves laterally for six weeks undetected.
scenarios.prompt: Which zero-trust principle was violated, and what replaces the VPN-centric model?
evidence: NIST's Zero Trust Architecture publication defines the core tenet: never trust, always verify. Access decisions are made per-session based on identity, device posture, and context — not on network location. 'Inside the network' is not a security property.
choices: Implicit trust by network location: the fix is identity- and context-based per-request authorization (a policy decision point evaluating user, device health, and resource sensitivity every session) instead of a one-time VPN gate with a trusted interior.
The principle of least privilege was violated; the fix is a bigger VPN with more bandwidth.
No principle was violated; VPNs are zero-trust by definition.
The violated principle is defense in depth; the fix is a second VPN inside the first.
scenarios.why: A VPN moves the perimeter; zero trust removes it. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted based on who and what is asking right now — location contributes context, never trust.
scenarios.hint: If the attacker is already 'inside,' what should still stop them?

scenarios.title: Build or buy the policy engine?
scenarios.situation: A mid-size firm must choose: build a custom policy decision point (PDP) in-house, or buy a zero-trust network access (ZTNA) platform. Build costs 2 engineer-years and full maintenance liability; buy costs $180k/year with vendor lock-in and a 6-month migration.
scenarios.prompt: How should they decide?
choices: Decide on differentiation and risk: access policy enforcement is undifferentiated heavy lifting with high breach cost if wrong — buy the platform (faster, maintained, audited) unless access control is genuinely a core competency; then run a pilot measuring policy-change latency, incident response integration, and exit cost before committing.
Always build; vendor products are never trustworthy.
Always buy the cheapest option; price is the only criterion.
Defer the decision for two years; the VPN is fine until then.
scenarios.why: The trade is build-risk (you own every bug in your PDP, and auth bugs are breach bugs) versus buy-risk (lock-in, price, fit). For security infrastructure, 'boring and maintained' usually beats 'clever and yours' — measure the pilot, price the exit.
scenarios.hint: Which risk is cheaper to be wrong about: your own auth code, or a vendor contract?

scenarios.title: The Core Idea
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks for a one-sentence definition of zero trust to anchor a new security program. Four candidate statements are on the table.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement captures zero trust correctly?
choices: Never trust, always verify — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and continuously validated regardless of network location
A strong firewall perimeter keeps everything inside it safe
All devices on the corporate LAN are trusted by default
Connecting through the VPN makes a device trusted
scenarios.why: Zero trust eliminates the idea of a trusted network: location on the LAN or VPN no longer implies trustworthiness. Every request — user, device, workload — must prove itself each time, because breaches routinely start inside the perimeter. The other options all restate the perimeter model that zero trust replaces.
scenarios.hint: What happened to the idea of a 'trusted' internal network?

scenarios.title: Beyond the VPN
scenarios.situation: A third-party vendor needs access to exactly one internal application for a two-week project. The traditional answer is a full VPN tunnel into the corporate network.
scenarios.prompt: Which access model fits zero trust best?
choices: Software-defined perimeter / zero-trust network access: brokered, per-application, per-session access with no network-level trust granted
A full VPN tunnel — it is how vendor access has always been done
Publish the application's port directly to the internet
Email the vendor the data they need instead
scenarios.why: A VPN grants network-level access — far more than 'one application' — and makes the vendor's potentially unmanaged device an insider. SDP/ZTNA brokers access to the specific resource only, after verifying identity and device, with no implicit trust in the underlying network. Least privilege applied to connectivity itself.
scenarios.hint: What's the least access that still gets the job done — a network, or an application?

scenarios.title: Trust, but Continuously Verify
scenarios.situation: A user authenticated normally from headquarters at 9:00 AM. At 9:20, a login for the same account arrives from another continent on an unknown device, and immediately attempts the admin panel.
scenarios.prompt: How should the architecture respond?
evidence: 09:00 MFA success — known device, HQ office
09:20 password-only success — unknown device, foreign ASN
choices: Step-up authentication and session re-evaluation — continuous verification challenges or revokes the session when risk signals appear mid-session
Do nothing — the session is valid for 8 hours once authenticated
Permanently block the user — no investigation needed
Only authenticate at login — that is the industry standard
scenarios.why: Zero trust treats authentication as a moment and authorization as continuous: the policy engine re-evaluates trust as context changes. Impossible travel plus a new device plus privilege escalation is exactly the signal set that should trigger step-up auth or session termination. Login-time-only checks leave an eight-hour window for the attacker.
scenarios.hint: Authentication is a moment — what should authorization be?

scenarios.title: The Policy Engine Decision
scenarios.situation: You are designing access policy for the finance application. Options range from a static IP allowlist to a fully dynamic model, and the team worries about complexity.
scenarios.prompt: Which model aligns with zero trust, and why is the complexity worth it?
choices: Attribute-based dynamic policy — user identity, device posture, location, and risk score evaluated per session by the policy engine; it adapts to real-time risk instead of freezing yesterday's assumptions
A static IP allowlist — simple to understand and audit
Identical access for everyone — fairness and simplicity
Annual access reviews only — least administrative overhead
scenarios.why: NIST SP 800-207's tenets require access determined by dynamic policy: the observable state of the identity, the device, and behavioral attributes, evaluated per session. Static rules cannot react to compromised credentials or devices — they encode trust decisions that go stale. The complexity is the point: it is what makes access decisions reflect current reality.
scenarios.hint: NIST says access is determined by dynamic policy — what does 'dynamic' have to buy you?

choices: SMS codes — they're MFA and everyone has a phone
Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn, smart cards): resists credential replay and adversary-in-the-middle, unlike SMS and push which are phishable
Push notifications — convenient and secure enough
Security questions as second factor
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker need to defeat each option — and which one can't be phished?
scenarios.prompt: Which MFA should protect the domain admins, and why?
scenarios.situation: Admins currently use passwords plus SMS codes. A recent adversary-in-the-middle phishing kit targeted the company.
scenarios.title: MFA that survives phishing
scenarios.why: Not all MFA is equal: SMS and push are phishable via adversary-in-the-middle proxies that relay the real session. FIDO2/WebAuthn binds the authentication to the legitimate origin cryptographically — the phish site can't replay it. For privileged accounts, 'MFA' must mean phishing-resistant MFA; anything less is a speed bump, not a control.

choices: Admins need convenience — let them browse from admin accounts
Privileged access workstations (hardened, dedicated admin hosts) plus just-in-time elevation: admin credentials never touch regular workstations or the internet
Give every admin a second laptop with no restrictions
Admin from the admin's phone
scenarios.hint: Where do credential-theft attacks harvest admin credentials — and what would make that well dry?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct privileged-access design?
scenarios.situation: Domain admins currently log in from their daily-use laptops, which also browse the web and read email.
scenarios.title: Admins on dirty workstations
scenarios.why: Credential theft (Mimikatz-style, token theft) harvests whatever is in memory on the compromised box — if that's a domain admin session, it's game over. PAWs (hardened, dedicated, no internet/email) plus just-in-time elevation (rights exist only when needed, then vanish) break the theft chain. Admin convenience never outranks the keys to the kingdom.

choices: Reset the user's password and move on

Treat as identity compromise until proven otherwise: revoke sessions/tokens, force re-auth with phishing-resistant MFA, investigate the sign-in context, hunt for persistence (new MFA methods, mail rules, OAuth grants)
It's just travel — ignore it
Disable the account permanently
scenarios.hint: What can an attacker do with a valid session that a password reset doesn't undo?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
scenarios.situation: Conditional access flags impossible travel for a finance director, followed by a new MFA method registration from the 'new' location.
scenarios.title: The traveling director
scenarios.why: Impossible travel plus a new MFA registration is the account-takeover signature — the attacker is cementing persistence. Password reset alone leaves stolen session tokens and OAuth grants valid. Full response: revoke everything, re-establish identity with strong MFA, and hunt the persistence mechanisms (mail forwarding rules, new devices, consented apps) before declaring it clean.

choices: More frequent password changes — 30 days keeps attackers guessing
Long, unique passwords with a manager plus phishing-resistant MFA; stop expiring passwords arbitrarily (per current NIST guidance) and monitor for compromised credentials
Passwords don't matter anymore
Require 8 characters with complexity
scenarios.hint: What does forced rotation actually produce — stronger passwords, or 'Winter2026!'?
scenarios.prompt: What does modern guidance say?
scenarios.situation: The password policy still requires 90-day rotation with complexity rules. Helpdesk is drowning in reset tickets.
scenarios.title: The 90-day hamster wheel
scenarios.why: Current NIST guidance (800-63) reversed the old dogma: arbitrary expiration produces predictable, weak passwords and huge support cost without security gain. The modern stack is: long memorable passwords (or better, a manager), no periodic rotation unless compromise is suspected, MFA (phishing-resistant for privileged), and screening new passwords against known-compromised lists. Convenience and security finally agree.

choices: Audit it annually — AD is stable
Treat AD attack paths as a continuous problem: audit privileged groups, Kerberoastable accounts, unconstrained delegation, and stale admins regularly; assume the paths exist and monitor for their use
AD can't be secured — migrate everything to cloud
Only worry about domain admins
scenarios.hint: How many hops is the average user from domain admin — and who mapped that?
scenarios.prompt: What is the defensive posture for Active Directory?
scenarios.situation: A BloodHound-style analysis shows the average user is 4 hops from Domain Admin via nested groups and misconfigurations.
scenarios.title: Four hops to domain admin
scenarios.why: AD's complexity creates standing attack paths — nested groups, delegation misconfigs, Kerberoastable SPNs — that attackers map in minutes. Defense is continuous hygiene (prune privileged groups, kill unconstrained delegation, remove stale admins) plus monitoring for the techniques (not just the paths). In zero trust terms: AD is the identity plane, and its paths are your trust assumptions made visible.

choices: Grant standing access — the team is trusted
Just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, time-boxed rights, and full session logging; standing privilege is the risk
Give them local admin on their laptops instead
Elevation is too slow for incident response
scenarios.hint: What is the attacker's window if the privilege only exists for two hours with approval?
scenarios.prompt: What is the zero-trust answer for third-party/vendor access?
scenarios.situation: A vendor needs occasional domain admin-level access for maintenance.
scenarios.title: The vendor needs admin
scenarios.why: Standing vendor admin accounts are a standing invitation — compromised vendor, compromised you. JIT elevation shrinks the window to the actual maintenance period, adds approval and logging, and removes the always-on target. 'Trusted vendor' is exactly the implicit trust zero trust eliminates; verify each elevation, every time.

scenarios.title: Whose laptop is that?
scenarios.situation: A contractor's personal laptop — no disk encryption, OS two years out of date — authenticates with valid credentials and receives full access to the customer database because the access policy checks only username and password.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the access decision?
evidence: Zero trust evaluates the subject AND the device: managed status, encryption, patch level, EDR health. Credentials prove who claims to be asking; posture proves what is asking — an untrusted device with valid credentials is still untrusted.
choices: Device trust evaluation: the policy must check device posture (managed, encrypted, patched, EDR-healthy) alongside identity — valid credentials on an unmanaged, unpatched device should get limited or no access to sensitive data.
Nothing is missing; valid credentials are sufficient for full access.
The contractor needs a stronger password; device state is irrelevant.
The database should be moved to the contractor's laptop for convenience.
scenarios.why: Identity answers 'who'; posture answers 'on what.' A policy that asks only the first question grants the keys to whoever holds the password, on whatever device they happen to own.
scenarios.hint: The credentials are valid — so what else must be true before access is granted?

scenarios.title: The service account that never sleeps
scenarios.situation: An audit finds a CI/CD service account with standing Domain Admin rights, a password unchanged in four years, used by twelve pipelines — three of which were decommissioned. The team says 'it works, don't touch it.'
scenarios.prompt: Apply least privilege and assume breach: what is the remediation plan?
choices: Eliminate standing privilege: inventory which pipelines actually need the account, scope each to just-in-time, time-bound, least-privilege credentials (short-lived tokens per pipeline), rotate or vault the secret, and remove the dead pipelines' access — 'it works' is not a security posture.
Change the password once and leave everything else as-is; rotation alone satisfies least privilege.
Grant the account Enterprise Admin so pipelines never hit permission errors.
Delete the CI/CD system; pipelines are inherently insecure.
scenarios.why: Standing privilege is pre-authorized breach: every always-on admin credential is an attacker asset waiting to be stolen. Just-in-time, scoped, expiring access gives pipelines what they need for minutes, not forever.
scenarios.hint: What does each pipeline need, for how long, and why does it still have it?

scenarios.title: Identity Is the Perimeter
scenarios.situation: The company is now mostly remote. The old model — VPN into the office network, then broad internal access — has produced two incidents from compromised home machines this year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right first control to deploy?
evidence: Incident 1: compromised home PC -> VPN -> lateral movement to file shares.
Incident 2: stolen VPN credentials used from unknown device.
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA plus device posture checks, enforced per application session before any resource access
Longer, more complex VPN passwords
A larger, faster perimeter firewall
A policy trusting employee home Wi-Fi networks
scenarios.why: When the network cannot be trusted, identity and device health become the boundary. MFA (preferably phishing-resistant) proves who is asking; posture checks prove the device is healthy; per-session enforcement means trust is re-evaluated continuously. Longer VPN passwords do nothing against a compromised endpoint or stolen session.
scenarios.hint: If the network can't be trusted, what becomes the boundary?

choices: One flat network — segmentation slows the business
Segment by trust and function: isolate crown jewels, OT, and user segments; enforce with firewalls/ACLs; verify policy actually blocks (test it)
VLANs alone without enforcement between them
Segment only the guest Wi-Fi
scenarios.hint: What does a VLAN buy you if traffic flows freely between them?
scenarios.prompt: What does effective segmentation require?
scenarios.situation: The network is flat: workstations, servers, and building controls share one broadcast domain.
scenarios.title: The flat network
scenarios.why: Segmentation is enforcement, not labeling: VLANs without inter-VLAN access control are just documentation. Effective design groups by trust/function, puts policy enforcement (firewall/ACL) between segments, and — critically — tests that the policy actually denies. Untested segmentation is a diagram, not a control.

choices: Network firewalls between servers — that's enough
Host-based microsegmentation: policy follows the workload (host firewall rules, identity-aware), enforced regardless of network location — because east-west traffic is where lateral movement lives
More VLANs — quantity equals security
Microsegmentation is only for cloud
scenarios.hint: Where does lateral movement happen — at the perimeter, or server-to-server?
scenarios.prompt: What controls lateral movement between servers?
scenarios.situation: Perimeter firewalls are solid, but a compromised web server reached the database directly — no control inspected that path.
scenarios.title: East-west blindness
scenarios.why: Perimeter firewalls see north-south; attackers live east-west. Microsegmentation pushes enforcement to the workload (host firewalls, service-identity policies) so server-to-server traffic is authorized per policy, not trusted by subnet. The web→DB path should have been an explicit allow, not an accident of flatness.

choices: It's fine — the vendor needs access
Isolate OT on its own segment with strictly controlled, monitored conduits to IT; no direct internet; treat OT protocols' lack of auth as a design constraint
Put OT on the corporate LAN for easier management
Air gaps are the only answer
scenarios.hint: What happens when the flat IT network's ransomware reaches the plant floor?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct IT/OT boundary design?
scenarios.situation: Manufacturing OT devices sit on the corporate network for 'easy remote management.'
scenarios.title: The plant floor on the LAN
scenarios.why: OT devices often can't be patched or authenticated — their insecurity is a design constraint, not a fixable bug. The answer is architectural: dedicated OT segments, tightly controlled conduits (data diodes or filtered firewalls for only required flows), no internet path, and monitoring of the boundary. Convenience access that lets ransomware reach the plant floor is the failure mode.

choices: Draw the diagram and declare victory
Test enforcement: attempt the denied flows from each segment, verify logging of both allowed and denied traffic, and re-test after every change
Testing is the red team's job
Annual review is sufficient
scenarios.hint: How do you know the firewall rule does what you think it does?
scenarios.prompt: How do you prove segmentation works?
scenarios.situation: The new segmentation is deployed. Leadership asks for assurance it's effective.
scenarios.title: Prove the walls hold
scenarios.why: Untested policy is hope. Validation means actively attempting denied flows from each segment, confirming allowed flows still work (no business breakage), and verifying both sides log correctly. Re-test after changes — segmentation drifts as firewall rules accumulate exceptions. 'We deployed it' is not evidence; test results are.

choices: Allow all east-west and monitor only
Default-deny between segments with explicit allows for required flows, discovered by baselining actual traffic before enforcing
Block everything and let the business file tickets
Segmentation doesn't apply to cloud
scenarios.hint: How do you learn what the app actually needs before you start denying?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe path to default-deny between segments?
scenarios.situation: You need to segment a legacy app nobody fully understands, without breaking it.
scenarios.title: Segmenting the mystery app
scenarios.why: Default-deny on unknown traffic breaks the business; allow-all teaches nothing. The professional path: baseline first (capture actual flows for a representative period), build allows from observed legitimate traffic, enforce in monitor/alert mode, then flip to deny. Discovery before enforcement is what makes segmentation survivable on legacy systems.

choices: The DMZ is obsolete in zero trust
A properly enforced DMZ still has a role: internet-facing services isolated from the interior, with no direct interior trust — but each service inside the DMZ still gets its own verification
Put the database in the DMZ for performance
DMZ means no firewall needed
scenarios.hint: Does zero trust remove the concept of 'facing the internet is riskier' — or refine it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the DMZ's place in a zero-trust architecture?
scenarios.situation: The team debates whether the DMZ concept survives the move to zero trust.
scenarios.title: DMZ in zero trust
scenarios.why: Zero trust refines rather than abolishes the DMZ: internet-facing services remain the most exposed and belong in an isolated segment with no implicit interior access. What changes is that the DMZ interior isn't trusted either — each service still verifies per request. The DMZ becomes one more micro-perimeter, not the perimeter.

scenarios.title: Flatland
scenarios.situation: A network scan shows 2,000 hosts on a single flat /16 with no internal segmentation. Server, workstation, printer, and IoT camera traffic all mix freely; any compromised host can reach any other on any port.
scenarios.prompt: What is the misconfiguration, and what is the fix?
evidence: Zero-trust architectures shrink implicit trust zones to the smallest practical scope — ideally per-workload — so a compromised host cannot move laterally. Flat networks grant every foothold the whole estate.
choices: Missing microsegmentation: the flat /16 gives every compromised host unrestricted lateral reach — segment by workload sensitivity (servers, workstations, IoT/printers isolated with default-deny between zones) so a foothold stays a foothold.
The subnet is too large; renumbering to a /24 will fix lateral movement.
Printers need static IPs; DHCP is the vulnerability.
There is no misconfiguration; flat networks are recommended for performance.
scenarios.why: Segmentation is blast-radius engineering: assume breach, then make sure the breach cannot walk. Default-deny between zones turns one compromised camera into an incident instead of an enterprise-wide event.
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker's second step require that you can deny?

choices: TLS on the login page only — that's where credentials go
TLS everywhere: all internal and external traffic encrypted, with HSTS and modern cipher suites — credentials, tokens, and data all traverse the network
Encryption is too slow for internal traffic
Only encrypt what compliance names
scenarios.hint: What else travels the network besides the login form — and what does a sniffer see?
scenarios.prompt: What is the zero-trust encryption posture?
scenarios.situation: The app encrypts the login page but serves the rest over HTTP 'for performance.'
scenarios.title: HTTPS on the login page only
scenarios.why: Session tokens, API calls, and data all traverse the network after login — HTTP anywhere leaks them to any sniffer (or compromised switch). 'TLS everywhere' including east-west internal traffic is the zero-trust baseline; the performance argument died with modern hardware and TLS 1.3. Partial encryption protects the front door and leaves the windows open.

choices: It's overkill — TLS already encrypts
mTLS: both sides present certificates, so services authenticate each other — critical for service-to-service trust without implicit network trust
mTLS replaces the need for any authorization
Only use mTLS for databases
scenarios.hint: TLS proves the server to the client — but what proves the client to the server, when the 'client' is another service?
scenarios.prompt: Why does zero trust push mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic?
scenarios.situation: Microservices currently trust any caller on the internal network.
scenarios.title: Who are you, service?
scenarios.why: In zero trust, workloads have identities too — IP addresses aren't identity. mTLS gives each service a cryptographic identity (certificate) verified on every connection, replacing 'it's on the internal network so it's fine.' Combined with short-lived certs and automated rotation, it's the foundation of service-mesh security.

choices: Encrypt the disk and call it done
Layered: encryption at rest (with keys in an HSM/KMS, not on the same disk), TLS in transit, and field-level encryption for the most sensitive fields — each layer addresses a different threat
Encryption at rest is enough for everything
Only encrypt backups
scenarios.hint: What does disk encryption protect against — and what doesn't it stop?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct encryption design for customer PII?
scenarios.situation: Customer PII lives in a database. 'We have BitLocker, so we're encrypted,' the team says.
scenarios.title: Encrypted — against what?
scenarios.why: Each encryption layer answers a different threat: disk encryption stops the stolen-drive scenario; TLS stops network sniffing; field-level encryption limits what a compromised app or DBA can read. And keys must live in an HSM/KMS — encryption with the key on the same disk is a locked safe with the combination taped to it. Ask 'against what?' for every layer.

choices: It's fine — certs last a year, someone will notice
Automate the lifecycle: short-lived certs, automated renewal, expiry monitoring with alerts, and an inventory of every cert — manual renewal is the outage vector
Only monitor the public website's cert
Renew when the browser warns
scenarios.hint: What wakes you up at 3 AM when a cert expires — and why is it always the one nobody inventoried?
scenarios.prompt: What is the professional certificate management posture?
scenarios.situation: Last quarter, an expired internal cert took down the VPN for six hours. Nobody owned renewals.
scenarios.title: The expired cert outage
scenarios.why: Certificate expiry outages are a solved problem that keeps recurring through manual processes. The fix is systemic: automated issuance/renewal (ACME-style), expiry monitoring with escalating alerts, and a complete inventory — you can't renew what you don't know exists. Short-lived certs make automation mandatory, which is the point.

choices: Classify data first, then apply crypto proportional to sensitivity — not all data needs the same protection, but the decision must be explicit and documented
Encrypt everything with the same key — simpler
Classification is paperwork — skip it
Only classify what auditors ask about
scenarios.hint: What breaks when the 'encrypt everything' mandate meets the 10-year-old reporting system?
scenarios.prompt: How should classification drive cryptography?
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants 'everything encrypted' but the legacy systems can't all take it.
scenarios.title: What gets the strong crypto?
scenarios.why: Classification makes crypto decisions rational: crown-jewel data gets field-level encryption with HSM-backed keys; low-sensitivity data gets standard at-rest encryption. 'Encrypt everything identically' either breaks legacy systems or gets quietly ignored. Explicit, documented classification turns crypto from a mandate into a risk-based design — and gives auditors the mapping they want.

choices: The cloud provider handles keys — nothing to do
Understand the shared responsibility: know who holds the keys (provider vs customer-managed), enable customer-managed keys for sensitive data, and verify rotation and access logging
Keys in the cloud are automatically secure
Avoid cloud KMS — on-prem only
scenarios.hint: If the provider holds the keys, what can the provider (or its compelled disclosure) access?
scenarios.prompt: What is the key-management question for cloud data?
scenarios.situation: Sensitive data is moving to cloud storage. 'The provider encrypts by default,' the team notes.
scenarios.title: Whose keys?
scenarios.why: Provider-default encryption protects against physical theft — the provider still holds the keys. Customer-managed keys (CMK/BYOK) add the separation: the provider can't decrypt without your key service, and you get the audit trail of key use. The zero-trust question is always 'who must I trust, and for what?' — key custody is trust made concrete.

choices: Blocklist known malware — allowlisting is too restrictive
Default-deny execution: only approved applications run; everything else is blocked by default — the inverse of antivirus thinking
Allowlist the antivirus itself and call it done
Allowlisting only works on servers
scenarios.hint: What does the blocklist not know about — and what does that gap cost you on day zero?
scenarios.prompt: What is the core idea, and why does it beat blocklisting for high-value systems?
scenarios.situation: The team debates application control for the domain controllers.
scenarios.title: Deny by default
scenarios.why: Blocklists enumerate known-bad — they lose to every novel binary. Allowlists enumerate known-good — unknown code simply doesn't run, which stops zero-days, living-off-the-land binaries, and unapproved tools by construction. The cost is operational (managing the approved set), which is why it's deployed first on high-value, stable systems like DCs, not on every creative workstation day one.

choices: Block it silently — users don't need to know
A defined exception workflow: risk-assess the request, time-box or scope the exception, log it, and review it on schedule — with a fast path so users don't bypass the control
Exceptions prove allowlisting doesn't work — remove it
Let managers approve their own exceptions permanently
scenarios.hint: What do users do when the official path takes three weeks?
scenarios.prompt: The CFO needs an unapproved analytics tool for a two-week project. What is the right process?
scenarios.situation: Allowlisting is live. Exception requests are piling up and users are complaining.
scenarios.title: The exception queue
scenarios.why: Allowlisting fails socially before it fails technically — if exceptions take weeks, users bypass the control entirely. A fast, risk-proportionate exception workflow (assess, scope, time-box, log, review) keeps the control credible. Permanent self-approved exceptions are just holes; governed temporary ones are the pressure valve that keeps default-deny alive.

choices: It's just allowlisting with a fancier name
Ringfencing constrains what allowed applications can DO (which files, network, registry they touch) — even approved apps get least-privilege boundaries
Ringfencing replaces the firewall
Only useful for browsers
scenarios.hint: What damage can a compromised-but-allowed application do — and what would stop it?
scenarios.prompt: What does ringfencing add beyond allowlisting?
scenarios.situation: An allowed PDF reader was exploited. It launched PowerShell and reached out to the internet.
scenarios.title: The allowed app gone rogue
scenarios.why: Allowlisting answers 'may this run?'; ringfencing answers 'what may it touch?' A PDF reader has no legitimate need for PowerShell or internet access — ringfenced policies would have blocked both, containing the exploit. Together they're defense in depth for the endpoint: allowlisting stops unknown code, ringfencing contains compromised known code.

choices: Block all scripts — security first
Control the script interpreters: allowlist which scripts may run (signed/approved paths), constrain interpreter capabilities, and monitor script execution — scripts are the attacker's favorite tool
Scripts can't be controlled — give up
Only block PowerShell
scenarios.hint: Why do attackers love living off the land — and what would make the land barren?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle PowerShell, Python, and macros under default-deny?
scenarios.situation: Allowlisting blocks unknown EXEs, but attacks now arrive as malicious scripts using built-in interpreters.
scenarios.title: The script problem
scenarios.why: Living-off-the-land attacks bypass application allowlists by using trusted interpreters for malicious scripts. The answer extends default-deny to the script layer: constrained language modes, signed/approved script policies, and blocking interpreters where they're not needed (does the workstation need Python?). The interpreter is the new executable.

choices: Count blocked executions and investigate what was blocked: blocks of legitimate tools reveal policy gaps, blocks of malicious tools prove value — measure both
It's working if nobody complains
Count total blocks — bigger is better
You can't measure prevention
scenarios.hint: What does a rising block count mean — better security, or a broken policy?
scenarios.prompt: How do you measure whether allowlisting is actually working?
scenarios.situation: The allowlist has blocked 10,000 executions this month. Leadership asks if that's good.
scenarios.title: Measuring deny-by-default
scenarios.why: Raw block counts are ambiguous — they could mean stopped attacks or a policy blocking legitimate work (which drives bypasses). The meaningful metrics: malicious blocks (true positives proving value), legitimate blocks (policy gaps to fix), bypass attempts, and user-impact measures. Investigate samples from each category; the story is in the breakdown, not the total.

choices: Deploy to all workstations on day one — speed matters
Phase it: start in audit/monitor mode to discover the real application baseline, tune policy, pilot on tolerant groups, then enforce — with rollback ready
Audit mode is wasted time — go straight to enforce
Only enforce on servers and skip workstations forever
scenarios.hint: What do you learn in audit mode that you can't learn from the software inventory?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rollout sequence?
scenarios.situation: You're deploying application allowlisting to 2,000 workstations.
scenarios.title: Rolling out default-deny
scenarios.why: Big-bang enforcement on 2,000 workstations is a self-inflicted outage — the real application baseline always differs from the inventory. Audit mode reveals what actually runs (including the weird-but-legitimate); tuning closes the gaps; piloting proves the process; then enforcement with rollback ready. Default-deny is a change-management project wearing a security costume.

choices: The red team 'winning' by owning the domain undetected
Both teams improving: the exercise is scored on detection coverage gained and fixes shipped, not on who beat whom
The blue team blocking everything
Keeping the results secret so nobody looks bad
scenarios.hint: What is the organization better at the Monday after the exercise?
scenarios.prompt: What defines a successful purple-team exercise?
scenarios.situation: The red team owned the domain in four hours. The blue team feels defeated.
scenarios.title: Who won?
scenarios.why: Purple teaming isn't a competition — it's collaborative adversary emulation where the red team shows its techniques in real time so the blue team can build detections. 'Red won' with no detection improvement is a failed exercise; 'red succeeded, and we shipped six new detections and two architecture fixes' is the actual victory. Score learning, not owning.

choices: Run it silently — realism requires surprise
Get explicit authorization, define rules of engagement and safety constraints, coordinate with the SOC (or run it as a known exercise), and have a kill switch
Surprise tests are the only valid tests
Tell everyone the exact attack plan in advance
scenarios.hint: What separates an authorized adversary simulation from an actual attack — in the eyes of the SOC analyst at 2 AM?
scenarios.prompt: What must be in place before the exercise starts?
scenarios.situation: The red team wants to run a 'no-holds-barred' surprise simulation next week.
scenarios.title: Authorizing the adversary
scenarios.why: Unauthorized 'surprise' tests burn SOC trust, risk real outages, and can trigger law-enforcement or HR incidents. Professional adversary emulation has: written authorization, scoped rules of engagement, safety constraints (no production destruction), SOC coordination (white-box, or controlled blind with safety rails), and an abort procedure. Realism comes from technique fidelity, not from ambushing your own defenders.

choices: File it and move on — the exercise is over
Convert each red-team technique into a detection or control gap ticket: map to the technique, write or tune the detection, atomic-test it, and track to closure
Blame the blue team for missing it
Only fix the critical ones
scenarios.hint: What is the exercise's output — a report, or a set of closed gaps?
scenarios.prompt: The red team used four techniques the blue team never detected. What is the correct follow-through?
scenarios.situation: Exercise debrief lists undetected techniques: token theft, DCSync-style replication, and living-off-the-land scripts.
scenarios.title: From exercise to detection
scenarios.why: An exercise that ends at the report is entertainment. Each undetected technique becomes engineering work: map it to its technique, build or tune the detection, validate with atomic testing, and track it like any vulnerability to closure. The exercise's ROI is measured in detections shipped and gaps closed — that's the continuous improvement loop that justifies the next exercise.

choices: Test the technology — people always fail
Test the decision-making: walk through roles, communications, escalation criteria, and decision authority under time pressure — the technology gets tested in live exercises
Tabletops are a waste of time
Only invite the SOC
scenarios.hint: When the real incident hits at 2 AM, what breaks first — the firewall, or the conference call?
scenarios.prompt: What is a tabletop exercise actually for?
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants a tabletop before the live red-team exercise.
scenarios.title: The tabletop
scenarios.why: Tabletops test the human system: who decides, who communicates, what the escalation path is, where authority is ambiguous. Technology failures are found in live exercises; coordination failures are found at the table — and coordination is what collapses in real incidents. Include legal, comms, and executives, not just the SOC; the 2 AM call involves all of them.

choices: Number of attacks blocked — higher is better
Detection coverage against emulated techniques, mean time to detect/respond on exercise injects, and gaps closed per quarter — metrics tied to improvement, not vanity
Red team win rate
Nobody measures exercises
scenarios.hint: Which metric would still look good if the exercise taught the organization nothing?
scenarios.prompt: How do you measure a red/blue program's value over time?
scenarios.situation: The CISO asks for KPIs for the new adversary-emulation program.
scenarios.title: Measuring the exercises
scenarios.why: Vanity metrics (blocks, win rates) can look good while nothing improves. Program metrics should track capability growth: technique coverage over time, detection/response times on realistic injects, and remediation velocity on findings. The trend line is the story — 'we detect 70% of emulated techniques now, up from 30%' justifies the program.

choices: More tools — the blue team needs better products
Assume the red team will adapt: rotate techniques, emulate different threat actors' TTPs, and re-test previously closed gaps to prevent regression
Run the same exercise annually — consistency matters
Only emulate nation-states
scenarios.hint: What happens to last year's detections when this year's red team tries something slightly different?
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep the program from going stale?
scenarios.situation: Year two of the program. Last year's gaps are closed, but the threat landscape moved on.
scenarios.title: Year two
scenarios.why: Adversaries adapt, so emulation must too: rotate technique sets, emulate different actors' TTPs, and — critically — re-test old gaps, because detections regress as environments change. A program that repeats last year's exercise is measuring last year's threats. Continuous, varied emulation is what keeps detection engineering honest.

scenarios.title: The alert that cried wolf
scenarios.situation: An EDR console fires 400 'suspicious PowerShell' alerts per day. Analysts have started bulk-closing them without review. Last week a real ransomware precursor hid in the noise for three days.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
choices: Tune detection to the environment: baseline normal PowerShell use, write allowlisted rules for admin tooling, escalate only anomalous command lines (encoded commands, obfuscated scripts, unusual parents) — alert fidelity beats alert volume, and bulk-closing is the failure to fix.
Disable the PowerShell rule entirely; PowerShell alerts are always false positives.
Hire more analysts to close the 400 alerts by hand each day.
Uninstall PowerShell from all endpoints to eliminate the alert source.
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a detection-engineering failure: every unactionable alert trains analysts to ignore the actionable ones. Zero trust assumes breach — which only works if the sensors that detect breach are trustworthy.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem too many attacks, or too little tuning?

scenarios.title: After the Breach
scenarios.situation: Ransomware entered through one phishing workstation and reached 400 hosts in hours. The post-incident review finds a flat /16 network: any host can talk to any host on any port.
scenarios.prompt: Which architectural change best contains the next incident?
evidence: Single flat VLAN: 10.0.0.0/16 — workstations, servers, printers, OT adjacent. No east-west filtering.
choices: Microsegmentation — enforce least-privilege east-west policy between workloads so a compromise cannot move laterally
Buy more antivirus licenses for the endpoints
Segment only the guest Wi-Fi — the servers are the priority
Air-gap everything and end remote work
scenarios.why: Flat networks let attackers move laterally at will — the blast radius becomes the whole enterprise. Microsegmentation carves the network into small trust zones with explicit allow-rules between them, so one compromised workstation cannot reach the server tier. It directly addresses the observed failure mode: uncontrolled east-west movement.
scenarios.hint: The attacker moved sideways — what controls sideways movement?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Zerotrust as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Zero Trust Principles Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Zero Trust Principles is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Zero Trust Principles?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Zero Trust Principles issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Zero Trust Principles is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Zero Trust Principles supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Zero Trust Principles failure in Zerotrust.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Zero Trust Principles
evidence: All Zero Trust Principles components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.
