domains.name: Capstone: Harden a Network to Zero Trust

scenarios.title: The EDR that watches only
scenarios.situation: EDR is deployed on 100% of workstations with good detections. But it is not wired to anything: no automated isolation, no feed to conditional access, no SIEM correlation. The SOC works alerts 9–5.
scenarios.prompt: What is the integration gap?
evidence: Detects well; acts never (automatically). Signals stay in the console.
Friday 6 PM ransomware: detected in 2 min, isolated Monday 9 AM — by a human reading the alert.
choices: Detection without enforcement integration: the EDR's signals must DRIVE actions — auto-isolation on high-confidence detections, device-trust flips feeding conditional access (infected device = sessions die), and SIEM correlation for the SOC. The 63-hour gap between detection and isolation is the integration debt. EDR as a standalone console is a tripwire with no alarm bell
The EDR needs better detections
The SOC needs weekend staffing
Ransomware is unstoppable once it executes
scenarios.why: The EDR did its detection job in 2 minutes; the ARCHITECTURE failed for 63 hours because no wire connected detection to action. Better detections do not fix the action gap. Weekend staffing helps but humans will always be slower than automation for the mechanical steps (isolate, revoke). 'Unstoppable' is false — auto-isolation in seconds contains what manual isolation in days does not. The integration pattern: high-confidence detections trigger automated containment (isolation + session revoke) immediately, while the SOC investigates in parallel. Humans do judgment; machines do speed. An EDR whose signals cannot trigger access decisions is a security camera nobody watches on weekends.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between EDR detection and EDR integration?

scenarios.title: The unmonitored database server
scenarios.situation: EDR covers all workstations. Servers were excluded — 'too critical for agents, and servers do not get phished.' The breach: attacker pivots from a workstation to an unmonitored DB server, lives there 4 months, exfiltrates via the server's legitimate backup channel.
scenarios.prompt: What assumption failed?
evidence: Workstations 100%, servers 0%. Rationale: servers do not click links.
Lived on the DB server 4 months; exfil via backup traffic (never inspected).
choices: 'Servers do not get phished' confuses initial access with the full attack: servers are where attackers LIVE (persistence, staging, exfiltration) precisely because they are unmonitored and always on. The 4-month dwell on the DB server is the direct product of the blind spot. Fix: EDR on servers with server-tuned policies (different baselines than workstations), coverage metrics per class, and the backup-channel exfiltration as a lesson in monitoring legitimate paths
Servers need different EDR; the workstation product cannot do it
The backup channel should be encrypted
Workstation EDR should have caught the pivot
scenarios.why: Initial access is one phase; persistence, lateral movement, and exfiltration are the others — and they happen on SERVERS, which is why attackers move there. 'Too critical for agents' is 2010 thinking (modern agents are safe; test in pre-prod), and 'servers do not get phished' is true but irrelevant. The workstation EDR saw the pivot's source, not its destination — without server telemetry, the trail ends at the hop. Encryption would not have stopped the exfil (it was legitimate backup traffic). The fix is coverage parity with class-appropriate tuning: servers get EDR with server baselines (they do weird-but-legitimate things), and the coverage metric is reported per class so the 0% cannot hide behind the 100%. Attackers go where the EDR is not — so put it everywhere.
scenarios.hint: Why do attackers move to servers after initial access?

scenarios.title: The agent that was killed
scenarios.situation: An attacker's first action on each host: kill the EDR agent (stolen local admin). The hosts keep full network access for days — 'agent not reporting' is not a condition in any access policy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fail-open design flaw?
evidence: EDR killed via local admin; hosts operate normally, invisible.
No posture-freshness requirement; 'no data' treated as neutral.
choices: Fail-open on missing telemetry: killing the sensor must DEGRADE trust, not preserve it. The fix is posture freshness in policy — signal older than X (or absent) = non-compliant = reduced access — plus tamper protection on the agent (so killing it is hard) and alerting on agent silence (so killing it is loud). The attacker read your policy: 'no data, no problem' is an invitation to blind you first
Tamper protection would have stopped it entirely
Local admin should not exist on workstations
The EDR vendor's fault for a killable agent
scenarios.why: Every EDR agent is killable by a sufficiently privileged attacker — tamper protection raises the bar but is not absolute. Local admin on workstations is sometimes unavoidable (dev machines). Vendor blame misses the architecture: the SYSTEM must assume sensor failure (hostile or accidental) and fail closed. 'No data = neutral' is the flaw — in zero trust, trust requires positive, fresh evidence; absence of evidence is absence of trust. The layered fix: tamper protection (make it hard), silence alerting (make it loud), and freshness-gated policy (make it consequential). The attacker killed the agent BECAUSE the policy ignored the silence — fix the policy and the killing buys them nothing but an alert and a quarantine.
scenarios.hint: What should 'EDR not reporting' mean for access?

scenarios.title: The 500 alerts a day
scenarios.situation: The EDR fires 500 alerts daily; 2 analysts bulk-close them in 20 minutes each morning. A real ransomware precursor was closed in a bulk session — 'it looked like the others.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the fidelity crisis?
evidence: Ransomware precursor closed unread; detonation 6 hours later.
choices: Alert fidelity collapse: at 500/day with 1% signal, the rational analyst response is bulk-close — and the system trains humans to ignore it. Fix: tune ruthlessly (suppress the benign-by-pattern, escalate the rare-and-dangerous), measure fidelity per rule (true-positive rate), and get to single-digit daily alerts worth investigating. The precursor 'looked like the others' because the tuning made everything look alike. Fewer, better alerts beat comprehensive noise
Hire more analysts to read all 500
The analysts were negligent; discipline them
Buy the premium threat-intel feed for better alerts
scenarios.why: More analysts scale the eyeballing without fixing the signal ratio — 500/day will still be bulk-closed, just by more people. Discipline punishes the symptom (the analysts adapted rationally to an impossible queue). Intel feeds do not fix noisy behavioral rules. The math is unforgiving: human attention is the scarcest resource in security, and 500 low-fidelity alerts/day spends it all on noise. Tuning is the work: per-rule fidelity measurement, precision suppressions (scoped, expiring, owned), promotion of high-fidelity patterns, and a target (alerts per analyst per day in single digits). The ransomware precursor was a tuning failure wearing an analyst's name. Fix the rules; the analysts were never the problem.
scenarios.hint: Why does alert volume destroy detection?

scenarios.title: The auto-isolated domain controller
scenarios.situation: The new SOAR playbook auto-isolates ANY host with a high-severity EDR alert. At 3 AM it isolates a domain controller (false positive from a backup agent). Authentication starts failing site-wide.
scenarios.prompt: What is the automation-safety failure?
evidence: Auto-isolate on high severity, no exceptions, no human gate.
DC isolated → auth failures → bigger incident than the false positive.
choices: Automation without safety rails: critical infrastructure (DCs, and by extension any tier-0 asset) must be EXCLUDED from auto-isolation — or gated on human approval. The playbook automated the mechanics without modeling the blast radius. Fix: exception list for critical infra (isolate = page human immediately instead), severity+context gating (high severity AND non-critical asset = auto; critical asset = human), and a tested rollback (un-isolate fast when wrong)
Auto-isolation is too dangerous; disable it entirely
The EDR false positive is the real problem
DCs should not run backup agents
scenarios.why: Disabling auto-isolation surrenders the 3-second containment that stops ransomware — the baby with the bathwater. The false positive is inevitable (tune it, but never expect zero); the playbook must be robust TO false positives, not assume their absence. Backup agents on DCs are normal. The design error: automation applied uniformly to non-uniform assets. Critical infrastructure gets a different response path — immediate human page + pre-staged investigation, not auto-isolation. The general principle: automate the REVERSIBLE and LOW-BLAST-RADIUS actions broadly; gate the IRREVERSIBLE or HIGH-BLAST-RADIUS ones on context (asset criticality) or humans. And every automated action needs a one-click rollback — the 3 AM mistake must be undoable in seconds.
scenarios.hint: How do you automate response safely for critical infrastructure?

scenarios.title: The Linux blind spot
scenarios.situation: The fleet is 40% Linux (servers, dev machines). EDR covers Windows only — 'Linux does not get malware.' A crypto-miner runs on 12 Linux dev servers for 2 months, found by the cloud bill.
scenarios.prompt: What is the coverage fallacy?
evidence: 40% Linux, 0% EDR coverage. Rationale: folk wisdom from 2005.
2-month miner, detected by finance, not security.
choices: 'Linux does not get malware' was never true and is laughably false now: miners, ransomware (yes, Linux ransomware exists), and supply-chain attacks target Linux heavily — especially servers and dev machines (high value, often unmonitored). The cloud bill as a detector is the indictment. Fix: Linux EDR agents (all major vendors have them), with Linux-tuned policies, in the same console and the same signal-wiring as Windows
Linux is still safer; the miner is low-impact
The cloud bill monitoring worked; formalize it
Developers should not have servers
scenarios.why: 'Low-impact' miners are the least of it — the same blind spot hosts ransomware, data theft, and persistence for bigger operations. Bill-based detection is accidental, slow, and misses everything that does not mine. Developers having servers is the business reality. The folk wisdom died a decade ago: Linux is a premier attack target (servers hold the data; dev machines hold the keys — SSH keys, cloud credentials, signing keys). Coverage must follow the ASSETS, not the OS mythology: every endpoint class gets EDR, tuned for its baseline, wired into the same trust signals. The 40% blind spot was a choice — unmake it.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'Linux does not get malware' dangerous in 2026?

scenarios.title: The 4-hour cloud VM
scenarios.situation: Attackers spin up cloud VMs for 4 hours of attacks, then delete them. The EDR auto-enrollment takes 6 hours to deploy the agent ('it is in the image build pipeline'). The VMs live and die unmonitored.
scenarios.prompt: What is the ephemeral-workload gap?
evidence: 4-hour lifespan, attacker-controlled, no EDR (enrollment slower than lifespan).
Agent baked into images; image rebuilds take 6 hours.
choices: Enrollment must be faster than the workload's lifespan: for ephemeral cloud workloads, EDR deploys via cloud-init/user-data at boot (minutes), not via image pipelines (hours) — or via agentless/cloud-native runtime protection. The 6-hour pipeline made sense for persistent servers; it is architecturally incapable of covering 4-hour VMs. Fix the deployment MECHANISM for the workload class, and add cloud-control-plane monitoring (who spun up the VM? the API logs see what the agent never will)
Block short-lived VMs; they are suspicious
The image pipeline needs to be faster
4 hours is too short for real attacks
scenarios.why: Banning short-lived VMs breaks legitimate autoscaling and CI. A faster image pipeline still cannot beat a 4-hour lifespan reliably — the mechanism (bake into image) is wrong for the class, not just slow. Four hours is plenty for data theft, mining, or relay attacks. The fix has two parts: (1) boot-time enrollment (user-data/cloud-init installs the agent in minutes — the VM is covered from minute 5, not hour 6), and (2) control-plane visibility (CloudTrail/Azure Activity Log shows VM creation regardless of agents — 'who spun up 50 VMs at 3 AM?' is an API question). Ephemeral workloads need ephemeral-capable security: fast enrollment + API monitoring. Design the control for the workload's actual lifespan.
scenarios.hint: How do you secure workloads that live 4 hours?

scenarios.title: The IMAP bypass
scenarios.situation: MFA is enforced via conditional access for all users. But an attacker bypasses it entirely using IMAP with a stolen password — legacy auth protocols do not support MFA challenges, and no CA policy blocks them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the gap?
evidence: MFA required, all users, all cloud apps. Legacy auth: not blocked (no policy).
IMAP/SMTP/POP with password → full mailbox access, no MFA prompt.
choices: Legacy authentication bypass: protocols like IMAP/POP/SMTP cannot do MFA, so they sail past the MFA requirement — the CA policy has a protocol-shaped hole. Fix: block legacy auth explicitly (a dedicated CA policy: block legacy authentication for all users), migrate the stragglers (the scanner/printer using SMTP AUTH), and monitor sign-in logs for legacy attempts (they are attack telemetry). MFA without a legacy-auth block is a locked front door with the window open
MFA is broken; the attacker found a flaw
Disable IMAP for everyone immediately with no migration
The password was weak; enforce stronger passwords
scenarios.why: MFA works exactly as designed — the attacker simply used a door without a lock. Legacy protocols predate modern auth; they authenticate with passwords alone and cannot be challenged. The CA policy set is incomplete without the legacy-auth block; this is deployment 101 that gets skipped because 'something might break.' Find the somethings FIRST (sign-in logs show exactly which accounts use legacy auth — usually printers, scanners, old apps), migrate them (SMTP AUTH with modern auth, app passwords as a bridge, or exceptions with compensating controls), THEN block. And keep watching the legacy-auth sign-in logs after blocking — every attempt is someone probing the old hole.
scenarios.hint: Why does MFA enforcement require a legacy-auth block?

scenarios.title: The enforce-first outage
scenarios.situation: A new CA policy ('require compliant device for all apps') is enforced on Monday morning with no report-only phase. By 9:30, 300 users are blocked — their devices show non-compliant due to a misconfigured compliance policy (encryption required, but the check misreads BitLocker status).
scenarios.prompt: What deployment step was skipped?
evidence: Enforced immediately, all users, all apps. No report-only period.
The COMPLIANCE policy was wrong (BitLocker misread) — the CA policy faithfully enforced a broken signal.
choices: Report-only mode and signal validation: every CA policy runs in report-only first (days to weeks), and the underlying signals (compliance policies) are validated BEFORE the CA policy depends on them. The CA policy was correct; its INPUT was broken — report-only would have shown 300 would-be blocks on Friday instead of 300 real blocks on Monday. Roll back to report-only, fix the compliance check, re-validate, then enforce
The CA policy was too strict; loosen it permanently
Compliance policies are unreliable; do not use device conditions
Users should have reported the BitLocker issue sooner
scenarios.why: The failure chain: broken signal (compliance misread) → untested enforcement (no report-only) → fleet-wide outage. Loosening the policy permanently surrenders the security goal for a signal bug. Abandoning device conditions discards a core zero trust input. Users cannot report what they cannot see (their BitLocker was fine; the CHECK was wrong). Report-only exists precisely for this: it answers 'what WOULD this policy do?' without doing it. The discipline: new signals get validated first (is the compliance data accurate?), then policies reference them in report-only, then enforcement — with a rollback plan (disable the policy = instant recovery). The 9:30 outage was a deployment-process failure, not a policy failure. Process it.
scenarios.hint: What does report-only mode protect against?

scenarios.title: The traveling executive
scenarios.situation: The CEO is traveling internationally. The CA policy blocks sign-ins from 'unusual locations' — defined as outside the home country. The CEO is locked out of email during a board crisis. The helpdesk creates an exclusion 'for the CEO, permanent.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the balanced fix?
evidence: Hard block on non-home-country sign-ins, all users.
Permanent CEO exclusion just created — the highest-value target, now exempt.
choices: Risk-calibrated location handling: replace the hard block with step-up (unusual location → require phishing-resistant MFA + shorten session + alert), keep the block for impossible-travel (two countries, 10 minutes apart — physically impossible = always block), and kill the permanent CEO exclusion (replace with the step-up path like everyone else). The CEO's travel was PREDICTABLE (calendar integration or pre-registration); the policy should handle travel, not exempt travelers
The exclusion is fine; executives need access
Block all international sign-ins; travel can wait
Remove location conditions entirely
scenarios.why: The permanent CEO exclusion is the worst outcome: the most-targeted account now has the weakest policy — and 'temporary' exclusions for executives have a way of becoming permanent (this one was born permanent). Hard-blocking all travel breaks legitimate business. Removing location signals discards useful (if noisy) input. The calibrated design: location as a RISK signal, not a binary gate — unusual-but-possible location triggers step-up (strong MFA the CEO already has) and monitoring; impossible travel triggers block (no human flies 8,000 miles in 10 minutes). Pre-registered travel (from the calendar or a quick form) suppresses even the step-up. The executive gets access AND the policy keeps its teeth. Design for the humans you have — including their travel.
scenarios.hint: How should location signals be used: block or step-up?

scenarios.title: The break-glass in the CA policy
scenarios.situation: The emergency break-glass admin accounts are included in the 'require MFA for all users' CA policy. During an IdP outage, the team cannot use break-glass — it demands MFA from the dead IdP.
scenarios.prompt: What is the CA design rule for break-glass?
evidence: Break-glass subject to the same CA policies as everyone — including MFA requirements that depend on the IdP.
IdP down → break-glass cannot authenticate → no recovery path.
choices: Break-glass accounts are EXCLUDED from CA policies (the standard, documented exception): they exist for IdP failure, so they cannot depend on the IdP. The exclusion is balanced by extreme monitoring (any use = immediate alert), long random passwords (vaulted, split custody), and scoped permissions. This is the ONE permanent exception — everything else gets conditions; break-glass gets exclusion + surveillance
Include them; security policies apply to everyone
The IdP should never go down; fix the IdP
Use a different MFA method for break-glass
scenarios.why: 'Applies to everyone' breaks the recovery path it is meant to protect: break-glass exists FOR the IdP outage, so conditioning it on the IdP is circular. IdP resilience is good but 'never goes down' is not a design assumption (it just did). A different MFA method still depends on the authentication infrastructure being up. The industry-standard pattern: break-glass excluded from CA, with compensating controls that make the exclusion safe — monitored like a fire alarm (any use pages security), credentials vaulted with split knowledge, permissions scoped to recovery needs, and usage followed by mandatory review + rotation. Document the exclusion with its justification; it is the exception that proves the rule (and the rule is: everything else gets CA).
scenarios.hint: Why are break-glass accounts excluded from conditional access?

scenarios.title: The one-policy-fits-all
scenarios.situation: One CA policy covers all 200 apps: 'require MFA.' The intern wiki and the production database have identical access requirements. The auditors ask how access is proportionate to risk.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing?
evidence: Single policy, MFA for everything, no tiers, no device conditions, no session controls.
Crown-jewel apps protected identically to the wiki — and the wiki's friction annoys everyone equally.
choices: App-tiered CA design: tier apps by sensitivity (public/internal wiki → standard business apps → crown jewels), then calibrate per tier — wiki: MFA; standard: MFA + managed device recommended; crown jewels: phishing-resistant MFA + compliant device + session controls + risk-based step-up. The single policy both under-protects (DB) and over-frictions (wiki). Tiering is how 'proportionate to risk' becomes answerable
The single policy is simpler to manage; keep it
Add MORE requirements to the single policy for everyone
Tiers are bureaucratic; trust the MFA
scenarios.why: Simplicity that ignores risk is not simplicity — it is negligence with good manageability. Piling requirements onto everyone punishes the wiki users without adding proportional protection (and drives circumvention). 'Trust the MFA' ignores that MFA strength varies and that device/session controls matter. Tiering is the standard answer to 'proportionate': it makes the auditor's question answerable ('the DB requires THESE controls because it is tier 1; here is the tier definition'), it focuses friction where risk lives, and it gives the program a growth path (new apps get tiered on onboarding). Three to four tiers, defined once, applied forever. The one-pager that ends the audit question.
scenarios.hint: How do you make access 'proportionate to risk' demonstrable?

scenarios.title: The guest that never left
scenarios.situation: A guest account (partner vendor) was created 2 years ago for a 3-month project. It is still active, with access to 5 apps, no MFA (guests were excluded 'to avoid friction'), and no owner (the sponsor left).
scenarios.prompt: What is the guest-lifecycle failure?
evidence: 2 years old, 3-month purpose, no MFA, 5 apps, orphaned.
Unmanaged external identity with broad access — the classic third-party breach path.
choices: Guest lifecycle with teeth: time-bound guest accounts (expiry tied to the engagement, auto-disable), MFA required for guests (no friction exemptions — external users are HIGHER risk), scoped to specific apps (not 'all employees' groups), sponsored (named owner, re-certified quarterly), and access reviews that actually remove. The 2-year guest is 5 failures: no expiry, no MFA, over-scoped, orphaned, unreviewed
Guests cannot use MFA; the exclusion is necessary
Delete it now; problem solved
The vendor is trusted; the risk is low
scenarios.why: Guests CAN use MFA (their own IdP federated, or one-time passcodes — the friction argument died years ago). Deleting now fixes one account; the lifecycle still produces the next one. 'Trusted vendor' is not a control (their breach becomes your session — the standard third-party attack path). The five failures compound: no expiry (time), no MFA (strength), 5 apps (scope), no owner (accountability), no review (hygiene). The guest program: invitation with expiry + sponsor, scoped app assignments (never broad groups), MFA enforced, quarterly re-certification (sponsor confirms or it disables), and automated disable on expiry. External identities get MORE scrutiny, not less — they are outside your HR, your devices, and your culture. Treat them accordingly.
scenarios.hint: Why do guest accounts need MORE controls than employees, not fewer?

scenarios.title: The log nobody reads
scenarios.situation: CA sign-in logs exist and are detailed — but nobody reviews them. A month-long password-spray against 200 accounts is discovered during an unrelated investigation. The logs showed it all along.
scenarios.prompt: What operational practice is missing?
evidence: Complete, detailed, unreviewed. The spray was visible in sign-in frequency + failure patterns.
None — discovered accidentally, a month late.
choices: Sign-in log operationalization: automated detections on the log (password-spray pattern: many accounts, one source, failures; impossible travel; unfamiliar locations at scale), a weekly human review of the high-risk sign-ins, and alerting thresholds. The logs are the cheapest detection source you own — they are already collected, already structured. Unreviewed, they are an archive; operationalized, they are a sensor
The logs are too voluminous to review
Password spray is unstoppable
The IdP should block sprays automatically
scenarios.why: 'Too voluminous' is why detections exist — humans do not read raw logs; rules surface the patterns (and the spray pattern is one of the easiest to detect: low-and-slow or fast, it has a signature). 'Unstoppable' is false (smart lockout, CAPTCHA, risk-based blocks all blunt it). IdP auto-blocking helps but is not complete (and needs tuning to avoid locking out legitimate users). The practice: 3–5 sign-in-log detections (spray, impossible travel, new-country admin, mass failures), a weekly 30-minute review ritual, and the metrics (spray attempts blocked/detected per month). The month-long spray was not a tooling failure — the sensor existed and was ignored. Operationalize what you already collect before buying anything new.
scenarios.hint: What turns sign-in logs from archive to sensor?

scenarios.title: The spreadsheet of gods
scenarios.situation: IT keeps the 'admin passwords' spreadsheet on a shared drive: 30 privileged passwords, last updated 2019, readable by the whole IT team (40 people) plus anyone who ever had access. One ex-employee's access was never revoked.
scenarios.prompt: What is the exposure?
evidence: 30 privileged passwords, 7 years stale, 40+ readers, ex-employee access live.
Every password is compromised by definition — 40 readers + 1 ex-employee + 7 years of copies/backups.
choices: Total credential compromise: assume every password in that sheet is known — rotate ALL of them immediately (starting with domain admin and cloud root), vault them in PAM (no human-known privileged passwords going forward), revoke the ex-employee's access everywhere, and investigate for prior misuse (7 years is a long dwell). The spreadsheet is not a vault; it is a breach disclosure waiting to be read
Change the share permissions to limit readers
Update the spreadsheet with new passwords
It has been fine for 7 years; the risk is theoretical
scenarios.why: Tighter share permissions do not un-read the 40 existing readers' copies (or the ex-employee's). New passwords in the same spreadsheet repeat the pattern with fresh victims. 'Fine for 7 years' means 'undetected for 7 years' — the most dangerous sentence in security. Every password in that file must be treated as public: rotate everything, in priority order, and assume prior misuse until the logs say otherwise (check 7 years of privileged logons for anomalies — painful, necessary). Then kill the pattern: PAM-vaulted credentials, no human-known privileged passwords, checkout with audit. The spreadsheet's era ends today — with rotation, not with better sharing.
scenarios.hint: Why must every password in the spreadsheet be treated as compromised?

scenarios.title: The 24/7 domain admin
scenarios.situation: 12 admins hold standing domain admin, 24/7, 'because incidents happen anytime.' Their DAs are used for daily work (email, browsing) on regular workstations. One workstation is compromised.
scenarios.prompt: What is the blast radius?
evidence: 12 standing DAs, used daily on workstations, no tiering.
One compromised workstation → DA credential theft → forest compromise. The classic path.
choices: Forest-wide, by design: standing DA on a daily-use workstation means any workstation compromise becomes a forest compromise — the credential is THERE to steal (LSASS, tokens). Fix: eliminate standing DA (JIT elevation only, via PAM), enforce tiering (DA creds never touch workstations — Tier 0 admin workstations only), separate daily accounts from admin accounts, and rotate/rebuild from the compromise (assume forest compromise until proven otherwise — KRBTGT reset twice)
12 admins need DA; that is normal
The workstation EDR should have stopped it
Rotate the one compromised DA password
scenarios.why: 'Normal' is the problem: 12 standing DAs on workstations is 12 forest-compromise paths, and the industry learned this lesson a decade ago. EDR helps but credential theft often precedes detection (and the DA was THERE legitimately — nothing to detect until misuse). Rotating one password misses the other 11 standing DAs and the systemic pattern. The fix is architectural: no standing DA (JIT via PAM, minutes to grant), tiering enforced (DA creds physically cannot reach workstations — separate accounts, separate machines), and daily work on non-privileged accounts. And the incident response: a DA compromised on a workstation = assume forest compromise (KRBTGT double-reset, full hunt) — because the credential's power is total. Standing privilege is pre-authorized breach material.
scenarios.hint: Why is a DA credential on a workstation a forest-compromise path?

scenarios.title: The unrecorded midnight session
scenarios.situation: A PAM checkout at midnight is used to 'fix' the billing database — directly, with sysadmin, no change ticket. The session is not recorded ('recording was not configured for this path'). Monday: billing data is corrupted, and nobody knows what was run.
scenarios.prompt: What control failed?
evidence: Privileged DB access, no ticket, no recording, data corrupted.
Checkout worked; session control did not — the proxy path bypassed recording.
choices: Session recording as a mandatory control: privileged access without recording is unaccountable — the PAM must ENFORCE the recorded path (no direct DB connections with vaulted creds; all access via the recording proxy), and checkout should require a ticket/change reference. The corruption is now un-investigable: was it malice, error, or coincidence? Unknowable. Fix: close the bypass (rotate the cred so only the proxy knows it), mandate recording on all paths, require change linkage for prod data access
The admin made an error; retrain them
Restore the database from backup
Recording is surveillance; admins need trust
scenarios.why: Retraining does not recover the lost forensic record — the question 'what was run?' is permanently unanswerable, which is the actual failure. Backup restore recovers data but not accountability (or the lesson). 'Trust' is not a control for sysadmin on the billing DB at midnight with no ticket. The architectural fix: the vaulted credential is ONLY usable through the recording proxy (rotate it so direct knowledge is useless), checkout requires a change/ticket reference for production data, and session review is part of the change process. Recording protects honest admins too ('I did not run that' becomes provable). Privilege without accountability is not administration — it is risk with a login. The midnight bypass proves the control was optional; make it structural.
scenarios.hint: Why must privileged sessions be recorded even for trusted admins?

scenarios.title: The rotation that broke production
scenarios.situation: PAM auto-rotates the service account password for the payment app — but the app reads the password from a config file at startup only. Rotation happens at 2 AM; the app keeps running with the OLD password until its next restart... which fails authentication. Monday: payment processing down.
scenarios.prompt: What coordination was missing?
evidence: PAM rotates on schedule; app unaware until restart.
Stale credential + restart = auth failure = downtime.
choices: Rotation-consumer coordination: before automating rotation, map every consumer of the credential and its re-read behavior — then choose the pattern: staged rotation (new password set, old kept valid during cutover, app restarted in the window, old revoked), or better, eliminate the static secret (managed identity / vault API with dynamic creds). Rotating a credential that apps cache is manufacturing outages. The 2 AM rotation was 'working' until the restart revealed the design gap
Disable auto-rotation for this account
Restart the app nightly to pick up rotations
The app is badly designed; rewrite it
scenarios.why: Disabling rotation returns to the 4-year-password pattern (the original sin). Nightly restarts cause nightly blips and still race the rotation. Rewriting the app is the long-term answer but not the Monday answer. The missing step was consumer mapping BEFORE enabling rotation — a 30-minute exercise (where is this credential used? when does each consumer re-read?) that would have revealed the startup-only behavior. The patterns: staged rotation with coordinated restarts (for legacy you cannot change), or credential elimination (managed identity — no password at all — for what you can). PAM rotation is not 'turn it on and hope'; it is a migration per credential, with the consumer behavior as the design input. The outage was a planning failure wearing an automation costume.
scenarios.hint: What must be mapped before enabling automatic credential rotation?

scenarios.title: The auto-approved everything
scenarios.situation: The PAM approval workflow auto-approves all requests under 'standard' — which includes domain admin checkout, because the category was misconfigured. 200 DA checkouts last month, zero human reviews.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong?
evidence: Auto-approve 'standard' — DA included by misconfiguration. 200 checkouts, 0 reviews.
Standing DA with a 30-second paperwork delay — the approval is theater.
choices: Approval calibration: auto-approval is for LOW-RISK standard requests (with guardrails: time-bound, scoped, logged); privileged elevation (DA, prod write, cloud root) requires HUMAN approval — and the categories must be audited (the misconfiguration proves it). 200 DA checkouts with zero review is standing access with extra steps. Fix: recategorize (DA = human approval, always), review the 200 checkouts retroactively (were they legitimate?), and alert on approval-policy changes (the misconfiguration itself should have paged someone)
Auto-approval is efficient; keep it
Require approval for everything, including read-only
The 200 checkouts were probably fine
scenarios.why: 'Probably fine' is not a review — 200 unreviewed DA checkouts is 200 opportunities, and the retroactive review is now mandatory (sample them; look for anomalies). Efficiency that bypasses oversight on domain admin is not efficiency, it is abdication. Approving everything including read-only creates the friction that drives circumvention (calibrate, do not blanket). The misconfiguration is itself a finding: approval POLICY changes need alerting and review (who put DA in 'standard'? when? why?). The calibrated model: risk-tiered approvals (auto for low-risk standard, human for privileged, multi-person for break-glass-adjacent), categories audited quarterly, and every approval decision logged with the approver's identity. Approval is a control; theater is a vulnerability.
scenarios.hint: How should PAM approval tiers be calibrated?

scenarios.title: The cloud root in the wiki
scenarios.situation: The cloud 'root' (organization owner) credentials are in the team wiki 'for emergencies.' MFA is not enabled on it ('MFA breaks the automation'). It has never been rotated. The wiki is backed up to 3 places.
scenarios.prompt: What is the crown-jewel failure?
evidence: Org owner, no MFA, never rotated, in the wiki, backed up thrice.
Total cloud control — every resource, every account, billing, organization policy.
choices: The highest-privilege credential has the weakest protection — inverted from every security principle. Fix: MFA on the root IMMEDIATELY (hardware key, vaulted backup codes), remove it from the wiki (rotate first — the wiki copies are burned), never use it for automation (create scoped service principals; 'MFA breaks automation' means the automation was built wrong), and lock it down (no API keys on root, alert on any root use — legitimate root use is nearly never)
The wiki is internal; the risk is contained
Automation needs the root; keep it as is
MFA on root is inconvenient for emergencies
scenarios.why: 'Internal' wiki with 3 backups is not containment — it is distribution (every backup, every reader, every ex-employee with a copy). Automation on root credentials is the design error ('MFA breaks it' = rebuild the automation with scoped identities, which is the actual fix). Emergency inconvenience is the POINT of break-glass design (monitored, rare, deliberate — not convenient). The root/org-owner is the single credential whose compromise ends the company in the cloud: attacker gets everything, including the ability to lock YOU out (new admins, deleted logs). The hardening is absolute and immediate: MFA (hardware), no standing API keys, alert on ANY use, vaulted emergency access, scoped identities for all automation. There is no 'acceptable' weak root. Fix it today.
scenarios.hint: Why is the cloud root credential the highest-priority PAM target?

scenarios.title: The vendor with domain admin
scenarios.situation: A backup software vendor's support account is a domain admin 'for troubleshooting' — created 3 years ago, used twice, password never changed, no MFA, no monitoring.
scenarios.prompt: What is the third-party privilege failure?
evidence: Vendor DA, 3 years old, 2 uses, no MFA, unmonitored.
External party holds forest-compromise capability, indefinitely, invisibly.
choices: Third-party privileged access needs the full PAM treatment: time-bound (per incident/ticket, not perpetual), scoped (only the systems in the support case), MFA'd, session-recorded, and auto-disabled after. The 3-year DA is 5 failures: perpetual, over-scoped, unmonitored, unrotated, unreviewed. And the vendor's own breach becomes your forest compromise — their security is now your attack surface. Fix: disable now, re-provision per-incident via PAM with full controls
The vendor needs DA to troubleshoot; it is standard
'Used twice in 3 years' means low risk
Trust the vendor's security
scenarios.why: 'Standard' does not mean safe — vendors ask for DA because it is easy for THEM, not because the troubleshooting requires forest administration (it almost never does; scoped access suffices). Infrequent use does not reduce risk (the credential is valid BETWEEN uses — 3 years of validity for 2 sessions). Their security is unknowable and their breach is your incident (supply-chain attacks specifically target these trust relationships). The pattern: vendor access is provisioned per-engagement (ticket-linked, time-bound, scoped to the systems in question), through the PAM (recorded, MFA'd), and torn down after — with the vendor's access reviewed like any privileged grant. 'The vendor needs it' is the start of a scoping conversation, not the end of one. Default answer: no standing vendor privilege, ever.
scenarios.hint: How should vendor privileged access be provisioned?

scenarios.title: The salary spreadsheet in Public
scenarios.situation: A scan finds the salary spreadsheet in the 'Public' share, readable by all 800 employees. It has been there 6 months. HR is horrified; IT says 'someone must have mislabeled it.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the classification-process failure?
evidence: Restricted data (salaries) in Public, 800 readers, 6 months.
No labeling, no DLP, no audit of the Public share — 'someone' is unknowable.
choices: No classification enforcement at all: the failure is systemic, not individual — without labels, handling rules, DLP, and audits, 'someone' will always misplace sensitive data eventually. Fix: classify (salaries = Restricted, with the handling rules), contain (move it, audit who accessed it in 6 months — breach analysis), and build the system (labels + DLP + quarterly Public-share audits). Blaming 'someone' misses that the system made the error inevitable and invisible
Find who put it there and discipline them
Move it to the HR share; done
Restrict the Public share to fewer people
scenarios.why: Individual blame does not fix a system with no guardrails — the next 'someone' is already dragging a file. Moving it fixes the instance; the 6-month exposure needs breach analysis (who read it? 800 people could have). Restricting Public dodges the classification question (what BELONGS in Public?). The systemic fix: labeled data (so the spreadsheet declares itself Restricted), DLP that blocks Restricted-to-Public moves (so the mistake is caught at drag time), and audits that catch what slips through (quarterly Public-share scans). Classification is infrastructure: labels + enforcement + audit, or it is a poster. The 6 months of exposure is the tuition for building it.
scenarios.hint: Why does blaming 'someone' miss the point in misclassification?

scenarios.title: The renamed file
scenarios.situation: DLP blocks 'salaries.xlsx' from email. An employee renames it 'data.xlsx' and it sails through — the DLP rule matched filenames, not content.
scenarios.prompt: What is the DLP design flaw?
evidence: Rename → different filename → no match → exfiltrated.
choices: Content-aware DLP, not filename theater: effective DLP inspects CONTENT (patterns like SSN/salary structures, fingerprinting of registered documents, ML classification) — filenames are user-controlled metadata, trivially changed. The rename bypass proves the rule was cosmetic. Fix: content inspection rules, document fingerprinting for the crown-jewel files (the ACTUAL salary spreadsheet, hashed — any copy detected regardless of name), and test DLP with adversarial bypasses (rename, zip, retype) before trusting it
Block all xlsx attachments
The employee is malicious; investigate them
DLP cannot work; remove it
scenarios.why: Blocking all spreadsheets punishes the business for the control's weakness. The employee might be malicious OR just renaming for convenience — investigate proportionally, but the CONTROL failure is independent of intent. Removing DLP surrenders the layer. Filename matching is security theater: it stops the lazy and the accidental, not the intentional or the clever. Real DLP: content patterns (regex for SSN/CC/salary formats), exact-data matching / fingerprinting (register the sensitive documents; detect their content anywhere, any name), and contextual rules (unusual volume, unusual destination). And TEST it adversarially — the red team renames, zips, encrypts, and screenshots; your DLP should be validated against those, not against the happy path. A control untested against bypass is a hope.
scenarios.hint: Why must DLP inspect content, not filenames?

scenarios.title: The 12 copies
scenarios.situation: The customer list exists in 12 places: the CRM, 4 analysts' laptops, 2 email threads, a USB stick, 3 cloud drives, and a printed copy. The DLP covers the CRM only.
scenarios.prompt: What is the data-sprawl problem?
evidence: The breach surface is 12x the CRM; the DLP protects 1/12th of the data.
choices: Data sprawl defeats point controls: DLP on the CRM is meaningless when 11 uncontrolled copies exist. Fix: data minimization (why do 4 laptops need full copies? tokenize/mask for analytics), authoritative-source discipline (the CRM is the system of record — copies need justification + expiry), and discovery (find the copies: endpoint scans, CASB, email DLP). The 12 copies are the finding; each needs a disposition (delete, tokenize, or justify + protect)
Extend DLP to all 12 locations
The copies are convenient; leave them
Encrypt the laptops; that covers it
scenarios.why: Extending DLP to 12 locations (including a USB stick and paper) is fantasy — the control cannot follow the sprawl. Convenience is not a data-handling justification for customer PII. Laptop encryption protects the devices, not the email threads, cloud drives, or paper. The real fix is reducing the copies: each copy needs a business reason, and most will not have one (the analysts need tokens, not full PII; the email threads were laziness; the USB was 2019). Data minimization is the highest-leverage control — every deleted copy is risk eliminated, not managed. Then: the remaining copies get justified, labeled, and controlled. Count the copies quarterly; the number should go DOWN. Sprawl is entropy; fight it deliberately.
scenarios.hint: What is the highest-leverage control against data sprawl?

scenarios.title: The 10-year inbox
scenarios.situation: An executive's mailbox has 10 years of email, including customer PII, deal documents, and credentials (passwords emailed in 2018). eDiscovery for a lawsuit now must review it all — at enormous cost. Retention policy: none.
scenarios.prompt: What is the retention failure?
evidence: 10 years, PII + credentials + deal docs, no retention policy.
eDiscovery review of a decade of mail; breach exposure of a decade of data.
choices: No retention = infinite liability: without a retention policy (delete after N years per data type, legal holds overriding), every mailbox becomes a 10-year breach surface and a litigation cost center. Fix: retention policies by data type (3 years standard, 7 for financial, legal hold process for litigation), automated enforcement, and the credential cleanup (2018's emailed passwords are burned — rotate anything still valid). 'Keep everything' is not a strategy; it is the absence of one
The executive should clean their mailbox
eDiscovery is just expensive; accept it
Delete everything older than a year right now
scenarios.why: Manual cleanup does not scale and never happens (10 years proves it). Accepting the cost normalizes the dysfunction. Mass deletion during (or anticipating) litigation is spoliation — potentially illegal. The policy answer: retention schedules derived from legal + business needs, enforced automatically (the system deletes; humans do not have to remember), with legal holds that SUSPEND deletion properly (documented, scoped, released). The emailed passwords are a separate incident (rotate them; they have been in the mailbox for 8 years). Retention is risk management: every retained byte is breach exposure + discovery cost. The default should be deletion on schedule, not preservation forever. 'Keep everything just in case' is the most expensive sentence in IT.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'keep everything' the most expensive retention policy?

scenarios.title: The label nobody honors
scenarios.situation: Documents are labeled (MIP sensitivity labels deployed). But: the DLP ignores labels, the email gateway does not read them, and users label everything 'General' to avoid friction. The labels are decoration.
scenarios.prompt: What makes labels enforceable?
evidence: The labeling program exists on slides only.
choices: Labels need three things: auto-labeling (content-based, so 'General' is not the path of least resistance), enforcement wired to labels (DLP + gateway + access policies READING them), and friction for mislabeling (downgrade justification: changing Restricted→General requires a reason, logged). Labels that nothing reads are metadata; labels that drive controls are policy. Fix the wiring AND the default (default-deny labeling: unlabeled = treated as Internal minimum, sensitive content auto-escalated)
Train users to label correctly
More label options will help
Labels are bureaucratic; drop the program
scenarios.why: Training alone cannot beat the incentive ('General' = no friction — rational users choose it). More options multiply the confusion. Dropping the program surrenders the machine-readable policy layer. The fix is structural: make correct labeling the EASY path (auto-labeling does it for them), make mislabeling HARDER than compliance (downgrade justifications, audited), and make labels MATTER (the DLP blocks on them — suddenly 'General' on a salary sheet gets caught by content inspection anyway). The enforcement loop teaches: when the DLP blocks their 'General'-labeled SSN sheet, users learn what the labels mean. Labels are infrastructure — they need the same engineering (automation, enforcement, feedback) as any other control. Deployed-but-unwired is the worst state: cost without benefit.
scenarios.hint: What three things make classification labels real?

scenarios.title: The production data in dev
scenarios.situation: Developers test with a full production database copy — customer PII included. Dev laptops, test environments, and CI logs all hold prod PII. A dev laptop is stolen.
scenarios.prompt: What is the test-data failure?
evidence: Full prod PII in dev/test/CI — uncontrolled copies across the engineering org.
Stolen dev laptop = customer PII breach, from a test copy.
choices: Test data must not be prod PII: the fix is synthetic/masked test data (generated or tokenized — realistic without being real), with the masked copy refreshed from prod through an automated masking pipeline. The dev laptop theft is now a hardware loss, not a breach. 'We need real data to test' is answered by GOOD synthetic data (distribution-matched, edge cases included) — and the rare cases needing real data get the masked subset with approval
Encrypt the dev laptops; the data is safe there
Developers need real data; accept the risk
The thief probably just wanted the hardware
scenarios.why: Encrypted laptops reduce but do not eliminate the risk (the data is also in CI logs, test envs, and every other dev machine — the sprawl is the problem). 'Accept the risk' for convenience is how breaches happen. Thief motives are unknowable — assume the data is compromised. The industry-standard answer: test data is a PIPELINE (prod → masking/tokenization → dev), automated, with synthetic generation for the common cases. Masked data preserves test validity (formats, distributions, relationships) while removing the breach value. The exceptions (needing real PII to debug) go through approval + time-bound + audited access — not standing copies on 30 laptops. Every prod-PII copy outside prod is breach surface; the pipeline shrinks it to near zero. Build it once; every future theft is a non-event.
scenarios.hint: How do you give developers realistic data without prod PII?

scenarios.title: The printer with the memory
scenarios.situation: A leased multifunction printer is returned to the vendor. Its hard drive contains 3 years of scanned/copied documents — including HR records. No one wiped it. The vendor refurbishes and resells it.
scenarios.prompt: What data-lifecycle step was missed?
evidence: MFP with HDD, 3 years of document images, returned unwiped.
Resold with HR records intact — a breach via the supply chain.
choices: End-of-life data sanitization for ALL devices with storage: printers/MFPs (drives hold every scan/copy/print), returned leases, decommissioned servers, old phones. The fix: asset inventory noting storage-bearing devices, sanitization procedure per device type (wipe/destroy per NIST 800-88), vendor contracts requiring certified data destruction on return, and verification (it is not done until verified). The MFP is a file server with a paper tray — treat it like one
The vendor should wipe returned devices
Printers do not store data permanently
It is HR's fault for scanning sensitive docs
scenarios.why: Vendor goodwill is not a control (their process is unknowable; the drive was resold intact). MFPs absolutely store data — every scan, copy, and print job images to the drive, often unencrypted. HR was using the tool as designed. The lifecycle gap: decommissioning covered servers but not the 'peripherals' that are actually networked computers with disks. The fix: (1) inventory ALL storage-bearing devices (printers, MFPs, copiers — ask facilities, not just IT), (2) sanitization standard per NIST 800-88 (clear/purge/destroy matched to sensitivity), (3) contract language (vendor certifies destruction; you audit), (4) verification before release. The returned MFP is the audit finding that writes the policy. Every device with a drive gets an end-of-life procedure — no exceptions for things with paper trays.
scenarios.hint: Why are MFPs a data-lifecycle blind spot?

scenarios.title: The phish at 9 AM
scenarios.situation: 9:00 AM: user reports a phished credential (entered password on a fake login). The attacker may have an active session. The IR playbook's first step is 'isolate the workstation from the network.'
scenarios.prompt: What should the first 15 minutes actually prioritize under ZTA?
evidence: Credential phished, session possibly active, workstation possibly compromised.
Network isolation first — the pre-ZTA reflex.
choices: Identity-first containment: the attacker's power is the SESSION, not the workstation's network cable. Minutes 0–2: revoke sessions + disable the user (IdP) — this kills the attacker's access everywhere, including cloud. Minutes 2–5: EDR isolate the device. Then scope (what did the session touch?) and preserve evidence. Network isolation alone leaves the stolen cloud sessions alive — the ZTA playbook leads with identity because identity is the perimeter
Follow the playbook: isolate the workstation first
Reset the user's password; that ends it
Wait for the SOC to investigate before acting
scenarios.why: The pre-ZTA reflex (pull the network cable) made sense when the network WAS the perimeter — the attacker's access died with the cable. Under ZTA, the attacker's access is the SESSION (cloud apps, VPN-less paths), which survives workstation isolation completely. Password reset without session revocation is the classic miss (the session does not care about the new password). Waiting for investigation while the session is live is containment delayed. The ZTA first-15: identity actions first (revoke + disable — seconds, via automation), device isolation second, scoping third — all from the playbook's quick-reference card, not improvised. The playbook needs updating: its first step belongs to the old architecture. Update it.
scenarios.hint: Why does ZTA incident response lead with identity, not network?

scenarios.title: The scope nobody measured
scenarios.situation: Containment done (user disabled, device isolated). The team declares victory. Two weeks later: the attacker used the session's API key (never rotated) to exfiltrate data for 10 more days.
scenarios.prompt: What scoping step was missed?
evidence: User + device. Missed: the API key the session created/used, service credentials touched, OAuth grants consented.
10 more days of exfiltration through the unscoped credential.
choices: Full session scoping: a compromised session's blast radius includes EVERYTHING it touched — API keys created, OAuth grants, service accounts used, data accessed (from the access logs). The scoping checklist: list all credentials/tokens/grants associated with the identity AND the device, rotate/revoke each, verify. 'User disabled' is not 'session scoped' — the API key outlived the user because nobody inventoried the session's artifacts
The API key should have expired on its own
Disabling the user should cascade to API keys
10 days is acceptable dwell for API keys
scenarios.why: API keys often outlive the user session that created them (no linkage, no cascade — 'should' is not architecture). Expiry would have helped IF the key had a short TTL (it did not — design gap). Ten days of exfiltration is not acceptable by any standard. The scoping discipline: during containment, enumerate the identity's full artifact set (sessions, tokens, API keys, OAuth grants, SSH keys, service principals) from the IdP + app logs, and revoke/rotate EACH — with verification (attempt the old key; it must fail). ZTA's rich access logging makes this enumeration possible — USE it. The checklist exists because memory misses things under pressure. Scope completely, or contain incompletely.
scenarios.hint: What artifacts must be inventoried when scoping a compromised session?

scenarios.title: The ransomware that met segmentation
scenarios.situation: Ransomware detonates on a workstation in the ZTA-hardened network: EDR flags it in 40 seconds, auto-isolates the host, the user's sessions are revoked, and microsegmentation blocks its SMB probes. Total damage: 1 workstation.
scenarios.prompt: What worked, and what is the lesson?
evidence: Detect 40s → isolate 45s → sessions revoked 2min → SMB probes denied (segmentation) → contained.
1 workstation. Compare: the pre-hardening tabletop predicted 60 servers.
choices: The layered ZTA response worked as designed: EDR (detection) → auto-isolation (containment) → session revocation (identity) → segmentation (blast-radius limit). Each layer caught what the previous might have missed — defense in depth with MEASURED performance (40s/45s/2min are metrics, not adjectives). The lesson for the program: this timeline IS the ROI story — '1 workstation vs 60 servers' justifies every control's budget. Document it, present it, fund wave 2 with it
The EDR alone deserves the credit
Ransomware is getting weaker
One workstation is still a failure
scenarios.why: Single-layer credit misses the point: if the EDR had missed (it sometimes does), segmentation still contained; if segmentation had a hole, session revocation still cut the cloud paths. The layers are the story — any one can fail and the outcome holds. 'Weaker ransomware' is complacency (it is stronger; the DEFENSE is better). One workstation is not failure — it is the designed residual risk, honestly achieved (perfection is not the standard; measured containment is). The program lesson: capture these timelines as evidence. 'MTTD 40s, MTTC 45s, blast radius 1 host' is the language executives fund. Every successful containment is a funding event — if you document it. The IR report for this incident is also the program's best marketing.
scenarios.hint: Why is the timeline itself a program asset?

scenarios.title: The notification nobody sent
scenarios.situation: The breach is contained technically in 4 hours. Customer notification happens 3 weeks later — legal was not looped in until day 5, forensics was never engaged, and the CEO learns from a reporter.
scenarios.prompt: What non-technical IR element failed?
evidence: Regulatory risk (notification deadlines), reputation damage (reporter-first), legal exposure (no privilege via forensics).
choices: The communication and legal tracks: IR is not just technical containment — it is legal (engage counsel early for privilege + notification analysis), communications (prepared holding statements, no reporter-surprises), and regulatory (know YOUR notification deadlines BEFORE the incident — 72h GDPR, state laws, SEC 4 days for material). The 4-hour technical win was squandered by the 3-week notification lag. The playbook needs the call tree, the counsel number, and the deadline cheat-sheet on page 1
Technical containment is what matters; comms can wait
The CEO does not need to know early
Lawyers slow down response
scenarios.why: 'Comms can wait' is how 4-hour containment becomes 3-week notification — and regulators fine the timeline, not the firewall rules. The CEO learning from a reporter is a governance failure with a name. Lawyers do not slow response; EARLY counsel engagement (privilege, notification analysis) SPEEDS the legally-safe response — late engagement is what slows things (now every document is discoverable). The playbook's page 1: incident commander, legal counsel (24/7 number), comms lead, the notification-deadline matrix for your jurisdictions, and the rule (no external communication without comms+legal). Technical IR without the comms/legal tracks is half an incident response — and the half you skip is the half with fines. Drill the call tree, not just the containment.
scenarios.hint: What belongs on page 1 of the IR playbook (non-technical)?

scenarios.title: The tabletop that found the gap
scenarios.situation: Quarterly tabletop: 'Ransomware on the file server.' The exercise reveals: nobody knows who can authorize the network isolation, the backup restore was never tested, and the IR call tree has 3 departed employees.
scenarios.prompt: What is the tabletop's value?
evidence: Authority gap, untested restore, stale call tree — all found in a conference room, zero production impact.
Discovering these at 3 AM during the real ransomware.
choices: The tabletop found 3 critical gaps for the price of a meeting: that IS its value — safe failure discovery. Each finding gets an owner and a date (authorization matrix documented, restore tested this month, call tree updated quarterly). The tabletop is the cheapest control in the IR program: 2 hours quarterly prevents the 3 AM discovery of the same gaps. And the meta-finding: if THESE basics were missing, what else? — schedule the next tabletop for the gaps' gaps
Tabletops are theoretical; only real incidents teach
The findings are embarrassing; keep them quiet
One tabletop a year is enough
scenarios.why: 'Only real incidents teach' is tuition at ransomware prices — the tabletop teaches the same lessons for bagels. Hiding findings guarantees their recurrence (sunlight is the remediation). Annual is too sparse (the call tree rotted in less than a year). The value proposition is precise: tabletops convert unknown-unknowns into assigned action items, safely. The 3 findings are now 3 owned remediations with dates — that is the entire output format that matters. And run them quarterly with ROTATING scenarios (ransomware, insider, cloud breach, supply chain) — the variety builds the muscle memory that the real incident will draw on. The team that tablets together, contains together.
scenarios.hint: What is the output format that makes tabletops valuable?

scenarios.title: The logs that were wiped
scenarios.situation: During containment, an admin 'helpfully' rebuilds the compromised server from backup — destroying forensic evidence (memory, disk images, log gaps). The investigation stalls: no timeline, no attribution, no scope certainty.
scenarios.prompt: What IR discipline was violated?
evidence: Rebuild before forensic capture — evidence destroyed.
No timeline, no scope certainty, regulatory notification now based on guesses.
choices: Evidence preservation BEFORE recovery: the IR order is contain → COLLECT (memory capture, disk image, log export) → then recover. The helpful rebuild destroyed the investigation's raw material — and 'scope uncertain' is the most expensive possible outcome (notification must assume worst case). Fix: the playbook states it explicitly (no rebuild until forensics clears), the team is trained on it, and the tooling is pre-staged (capture tools ready, not downloaded during the incident)
The admin meant well; no harm done
Rebuilding fast minimizes downtime, which matters more
Forensics is optional for most incidents
scenarios.why: 'Meant well' does not restore the disk image — good intentions with wrong sequencing still destroy evidence. Downtime matters, but 'scope uncertain' extends the incident FAR longer than the capture delay (and the notification/legal exposure dwarfs the downtime cost). Forensics is not optional when scope determines notification obligations (it almost always does). The discipline: CONTAIN (stop the bleeding — isolate, revoke), COLLECT (capture the evidence — memory, disk, logs), then RECOVER (rebuild). The order is the control. Pre-stage the capture tooling and train the team that 'rebuild' is a forbidden word until forensics says otherwise. The admin's helpfulness is a training failure, not a character flaw — train the sequence until it is reflex.
scenarios.hint: What is the correct IR sequencing for a compromised host?

scenarios.title: The post-mortem that blamed
scenarios.situation: The post-incident review opens with 'who clicked the phish?' The user is named, shamed, and the meeting ends. No control gaps discussed. Next quarter: another phish, another click, another naming.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this post-mortem?
evidence: Repeat incidents — the blame changed nothing.
choices: Blameless post-mortems focused on SYSTEMS: the question is never 'who clicked?' but 'why did one click cause damage?' — which leads to the real fixes (phishing-resistant MFA so the click does not matter, EDR auto-isolation, session controls, training improvements). Blame teaches users to HIDE mistakes (the next phish goes unreported — far worse). The repeat pattern proves blame does not prevent recurrence; systemic fixes do
The user deserved it; accountability matters
Some people are just clickers; accept it
Post-mortems are bureaucratic; skip them
scenarios.why: Accountability for SYSTEMS, not individuals: the user is the last line of a defense that failed at every earlier line (the phish got through email filtering, the fake site was not blocked, the credential worked without MFA, the session had broad access). Naming the user fixes none of those — and guarantees the next click goes unreported (blame creates concealment, which destroys detection). 'Some people click' is true AND irrelevant — design for it (FIDO2 makes the click harmless). Skipping post-mortems surrenders the learning entirely. The blameless format: timeline, contributing factors (plural, systemic), action items (named, dated, systemic) — and the explicit norm that the user who REPORTED the phish did the right thing. The reporter is the hero of the story; write the story that way.
scenarios.hint: Why do blameless post-mortems outperform blameful ones?

lessons.title: Identity & AD Defense — Core concepts
concepts: Phishing-resistant MFA: for privileged accounts, 'MFA' must mean phishing-resistant MFA; anything less is a speed bump, not a control.
Privileged access: defense is continuous hygiene (prune privileged groups, kill unconstrained delegation, remove stale admins) plus monitoring for the techniques (not just the paths).

Tiered admin model: credential theft (Mimikatz-style, token theft) harvests whatever is in memory on the compromised box — if that's a domain admin session, it's game over. Standing vendor admin accounts are a standing invitation — compromised vendor, compromised you.

Identity compromise response: full response: revoke everything, re-establish identity with strong MFA, and hunt the persistence mechanisms (mail forwarding rules, new devices, consented apps) before declaring it clean.
Session revocation: password reset alone leaves stolen session tokens and OAuth grants valid.

East-west traffic: default-deny on unknown traffic breaks the business; allow-all teaches nothing.
OT segmentation: untested segmentation is a diagram, not a control. Re-test after changes — segmentation drifts as firewall rules accumulate exceptions.

lessons.title: Cryptography — Core concepts
concepts: TLS everywhere: 'TLS everywhere' including east-west internal traffic is the zero-trust baseline; the performance argument died with modern hardware and TLS 1.3.

Internal encryption: in zero trust, workloads have identities too — IP addresses aren't identity. mTLS gives each service a cryptographic identity (certificate) verified on every connection, replacing 'it's on the internal network so it's fine.' Combined with short-lived certs and automated rotation, it's the foundation of service-mesh security.
Service identity: customer-managed keys (CMK/BYOK) add the separation: the provider can't decrypt without your key service, and you get the audit trail of key use.
Defense in depth crypto: explicit, documented classification turns crypto from a mandate into a risk-based design — and gives auditors the mapping they want.

Key management: and keys must live in an HSM/KMS — encryption with the key on the same disk is a locked safe with the combination taped to it. The zero-trust question is always 'who must I trust, and for what?' — key custody is trust made concrete.

lessons.title: Allowlisting & Ringfencing — Core concepts
concepts: Allowlisting fails socially before it fails technically — if exceptions take weeks, users bypass the control entirely. Allowlisting answers 'may this run?'; ringfencing answers 'what may it touch?' A PDF reader has no legitimate need for PowerShell or internet access — ringfenced policies would have blocked both, containing the exploit.
Exception handling: a fast, risk-proportionate exception workflow (assess, scope, time-box, log, review) keeps the control credible.
Ringfencing: together they're defense in depth for the endpoint: allowlisting stops unknown code, ringfencing contains compromised known code.

Application containment: living-off-the-land attacks bypass application allowlists by using trusted interpreters for malicious scripts. Big-bang enforcement on 2,000 workstations is a self-inflicted outage — the real application baseline always differs from the inventory.

lessons.title: Red/Blue Operations — Core concepts
concepts: Purple teaming isn't a competition — it's collaborative adversary emulation where the red team shows its techniques in real time so the blue team can build detections.

Exercise goals: the exercise's ROI is measured in detections shipped and gaps closed — that's the continuous improvement loop that justifies the next exercise. 'Red won' with no detection improvement is a failed exercise; 'red succeeded, and we shipped six new detections and two architecture fixes' is the actual victory.

Rules of engagement: professional adversary emulation has: written authorization, scoped rules of engagement, safety constraints (no production destruction), SOC coordination (white-box, or controlled blind with safety rails), and an abort procedure.
Exercise safety: an exercise that ends at the report is entertainment. A program that repeats last year's exercise is measuring last year's threats.

Findings to detections: adversaries adapt, so emulation must too: rotate technique sets, emulate different actors' TTPs, and — critically — re-test old gaps, because detections regress as environments change.
Remediation loop: program metrics should track capability growth: technique coverage over time, detection/response times on realistic injects, and remediation velocity on findings.
