lessons.title: Start Here: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: Three content types: lessons (concepts with worked examples), scenarios (timed decision drills — read the evidence before choosing), and labs (hands-on terminal exercises with automatic checks).
Work each domain as a triad: lessons first, then scenarios closed-book, then labs. This bootcamp is implementation-focused: the labs prove you can DO zero trust, not just describe it.
Mock Assessment is your final exam — it draws from every domain at runtime. Attempt it only when every domain is green.
Systems Anatomy is shared fundamentals. Zero trust implementations fail on weak fundamentals (DNS, Kerberos, PKI) — do not skip it.

example.code:
Worked example — a 60-minute study block
Setup: 25 min lessons → 20 min scenarios → 15 min lab.
Reasoning: Load the model, test recall under pressure, prove with commands.
Takeaway: One triad pass per domain beats three passive re-reads.
example.walkthrough: Run one full triad on the Conditional Access domain today; log your three weakest topics.

pitfalls: Jumping to scenarios without lessons — the 'why' explanations assume lesson vocabulary.
Skipping labs: implementation skill is typed, not read.
Taking the mock first 'for a baseline' — it wastes your only dress rehearsal.
lessons.try_it: Pick a domain and complete its triad now.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: The Implementation Learning Loop
concepts: Learn in three layers: Layer 1 — the principle (why conditional access, why PAM). Layer 2 — the mechanism (the policy, the vault, the EDR signal). Layer 3 — the failure mode (what breaks, how you detect it, how you recover).
For every lesson ask 'how would I implement this on Monday?' If you cannot name the tool, the policy, and the verification step, you have theory, not skill.
Build a personal runbook: every lab's commands, copied verbatim. Implementation interviews ask 'show me' — the runbook is your rehearsal.
Revisit scenarios 48 hours after passing them. Conditional-access evaluation order and PAM checkout flows are the classic fade-fast details.

example.code:
Worked example — the Monday test
Setup: Lesson teaches EDR-to-access-decision wiring.
Reasoning: Ask: 'On Monday I would: check the EDR API, map health states to device compliance, write the CA policy, test with a lab device.'
Takeaway: Every lesson ends with a Monday plan.
example.walkthrough: After each lesson, write your Monday implementation plan in three bullets.

pitfalls: Theory without tooling: 'I understand PAM' but cannot name the checkout flow.
Studying controls in isolation: real implementations chain them (EDR → CA → PAM).
No runbook: untyped knowledge evaporates under interview pressure.
lessons.try_it: Start your runbook: one section per domain, commands and flows.

lessons.title: What Interviews and Exams Actually Test
concepts: Interviewers test implementation depth: 'Walk me through a conditional access policy you built,' 'How does your EDR feed access decisions?' 'Show me your PAM checkout flow.' They want artifacts and stories, not definitions.
Expect troubleshooting: 'A user is blocked by CA — diagnose it.' Answers must show the sign-in log, the policy evaluation order, and the fix — the actual tools, named.

Exam-style questions weight: CA policy components (assignments, conditions, grant controls), PAM patterns (vaulting, JIT, session recording), EDR signal mapping, data classification handling, and IR playbooks under ZTA.
The differentiator: the capstone. 'I hardened a lab network: here is the before/after, the policies, and what broke' beats every certification answer.

example.code:
Worked example — answering 'diagnose the CA block'
Setup: User blocked, needs the CRM.
Reasoning: Wrong: 'check the policy.' Right: sign-in log → which policy fired → which condition failed (device? location? risk?) → fix the condition or the device, verify, document.
Takeaway: Named tools, ordered steps, verified fix.
example.walkthrough: Answer three scenarios aloud in 90 seconds, naming tools at each step.

pitfalls: Describing instead of implementing: 'CA policies evaluate signals' vs 'here is mine.'
No troubleshooting methodology: guessing instead of log-driven diagnosis.
No capstone: implementation claims without an implemented thing.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself diagnosing one blocked-access scenario with named tools.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: From Principles to Hardened Network
concepts: Phase 1 — Control plane: conditional-access, pam. Goal: build working CA policies and a PAM checkout flow in lab.
Phase 2 — Signals: edr-integration, data-classification. Goal: wire EDR health into access decisions; classify and label a data set.
Phase 3 — Operations: incident-response plus the existing redblue/segmentation/cryptography domains. Goal: run an IR tabletop under ZTA assumptions.
Capstone: harden a lab network end to end — identity, CA, PAM, EDR signals, segmentation, and an IR drill. Documented before/after.
Pace: one phase per week, one triad per day.

example.code:
Worked example — phase gate
Setup: End of Phase 1.
Reasoning: Gate: show a CA policy blocking a non-compliant device (with the sign-in log as proof) and a recorded PAM checkout session.
Takeaway: Gates are demonstrations, not chapters.
example.walkthrough: Write your three phase-gate demonstrations now.

pitfalls: Skipping to IR without the controls: response assumes the architecture exists.
No capstone: implementation skill without an implemented environment.
Rushing Phase 1: CA and PAM are the foundation everything else signals into.
lessons.try_it: Schedule your phase gates on the calendar this week.

lessons.title: Capstone Brief: Harden a Lab Network to Zero Trust
concepts: Your capstone: take a flat lab network (or a realistic design) and harden it to zero trust implementation: identity with MFA, conditional access policies, PAM for admins, EDR with signal-wiring, microsegmentation, and labeled data — then attack it (red team) and defend (blue team).

Constraints that make it real: brownfield starting point (flat, password-only, standing admins), everything as code/config in git, every control verified by a test (not by belief), and a red-team exercise at the end.
Deliverables: before/after architecture, all policies as code, the runbook (CA troubleshooting, PAM checkout, IR playbook), red-team report, and the remediation log.
Grading: can the red team move laterally? How fast is detection? Show the logs.

example.code:
Worked example — the demo narrative
Setup: 'Show me the hardening.'
Reasoning: Before: flat, password-only, standing DA. After: CA blocks non-compliant, PAM vaults admins, EDR kills sessions on malware, segmentation contains the red team to one host. Evidence: sign-in logs, session recordings, firewall denies.
Takeaway: Before/after with evidence is the whole interview.
example.walkthrough: Write your capstone brief: starting state, target state, constraints, tests.

pitfalls: Starting from a greenfield: the hardening story needs a 'before.'
Controls without verification tests: belief-based security.
No red team: untested hardening is a hypothesis.
lessons.try_it: Create the repo and commit the 'before' architecture diagram today.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: The Implemented Stack
concepts: Identity: IdP with MFA (phishing-resistant for admins), conditional access policies per app tier, device compliance as a condition.
Privilege: PAM vault for all admin credentials, JIT checkout with approval, session recording, break-glass monitored.
Signals: EDR on every endpoint, health wired into CA device conditions; SIEM collecting the control-plane logs.

Network/data: host firewalls default-deny, tier segmentation, data classified and labeled with handling rules. IR playbook written for the ZTA reality (fast containment via identity/device revocation).

example.code:
Worked example — the access decision stack
Setup: Admin needs a server.
Reasoning: Request → PAM checkout (MFA, approval, 4h) → CA evaluates (compliant device? known location?) → session recorded → EDR monitors → anomaly kills the session. Five controls, one workflow.
Takeaway: The stack is the story — layered, verified, logged.
example.walkthrough: Draw your implemented stack: every control, every signal flow, every log destination.

pitfalls: One control per layer on paper but not implemented: the stack must be REAL.
Signals not wired: EDR installed but not feeding CA is decoration.
No log destinations: unlogged controls are unprovable.
lessons.try_it: List every signal flow: source, destination, freshness requirement.

lessons.title: Capstone Verification: Red Team vs Your Hardening
concepts: Verification: a red-team exercise against your hardened lab — phish a credential, attempt lateral movement, try privilege escalation. Blue team (you) detects and responds using the IR playbook.

Measure: time to initial access, lateral movement achieved (hosts reached), time to detection, time to containment. Compare against the 'before' state (run the same exercise pre-hardening if possible).
Evidence: the red-team report (paths taken, blocked, detected), the blue-team timeline (alerts, actions), and the remediation log (what you fixed after).
The honest artifact: publish what still failed. 'The red team reached X because Y; fixing it next' is more credible than claimed perfection.

example.code:
Worked example — the exercise
Setup: Red team gets a phished user credential.
Reasoning: Before: VPN + password → full LAN in 20 min. After: MFA blocks; with session theft: CA device check fails; EDR flags anomaly; segmentation contains to one host; contained in 35 min.
Takeaway: Measured improvement, honestly reported.
example.walkthrough: Plan the exercise: scope, rules of engagement, success metrics, dates.

pitfalls: Skipping the 'before' run: no baseline, no proven improvement.
Red team too gentle: the exercise must be realistic to be useful.
Hiding failures: the remediation log is the credibility.
lessons.try_it: Schedule the exercise; write the rules of engagement now.

lessons.title: Implementing Never Trust, Always Verify
concepts: Implementation checklist: inventory subjects (users, devices, workloads), enforce authentication at every PEP, authorize per session against policy, encrypt all flows, log every decision.
The migration trap: 'we verify at the VPN' is not per-session verification. Map every 'trust zone' in your network and replace each with an explicit verification step.
Workload coverage: service accounts and automation need the same treatment — workload identity, short-lived credentials, per-request auth. Users-only verification leaves the machine backdoor open.
Verification evidence: each verification should produce a log (who/what was verified, when, against what policy). Unlogged verification is unverifiable.

example.code:
Worked example — the zone inventory
Setup: List every place 'inside the network' grants access today.
Reasoning: File share ACLs by subnet, app with no auth 'because internal', flat DB access. Each becomes a verification point: identity + device + policy.
Takeaway: The zone list IS the implementation backlog.
example.walkthrough: Inventory your trust zones; convert the top one to explicit verification this week.

pitfalls: Verifying users but not service-to-service: the machine paths bypass everything.
One verification at the edge: perimeter thinking with new branding.
No verification logs: the implementation cannot be audited.
lessons.try_it: Pick one internal app with no auth; put a PEP in front of it.

lessons.title: Assume Breach: Implementation Patterns
concepts: Network: microsegmentation with default-deny (host firewalls first — cheapest, finest-grained), tier isolation, management-plane separation.
Identity: no standing privilege (JIT), phishing-resistant MFA for admins, service accounts vaulted and rotated.
Detection: EDR everywhere, east-west flow logging, canary tokens/credentials (a fake admin credential that alerts when used — the tripwire).
Recovery: tested backups (immutable), documented rebuild procedures, practiced IR. Assume breach includes assume-ransomware.

example.code:
Worked example — the canary
Setup: Deploy a canary credential (fake DA account, monitored).
Reasoning: Any use = compromise in progress — the alert fires before damage spreads. Cheap, high-signal.
Takeaway: Assume breach means building tripwires, not just walls.
example.walkthrough: Deploy one canary (credential, token, or file) this week; wire its alert.

pitfalls: Walls without tripwires: prevention-only, no detection of the inevitable breach.
Assume breach as a slide: it must produce controls, or it is marketing.
Canaries nobody monitors: the tripwire with no one watching the wire.
lessons.try_it: List your tripwires: what alerts when prevention fails?

lessons.title: Least Privilege in Practice: JIT and Scoping
concepts: JIT implementation: request portal or chatops, approval workflow (manager/auto for standard), time-bound grant (hours), automatic revocation, full session logging.
Scoping: role definitions from actual usage (mine the logs — what did this role DO last quarter?), not from job titles. Unused permissions get removed quarterly.
Break-glass: the monitored emergency path (alerts on use, credential rotated after). JIT handles the routine; break-glass handles the extraordinary.
Metrics: standing-privilege count (trending down), average grant duration, approval time, unused-permission removals per quarter.

example.code:
Worked example — the JIT flow
Setup: Developer needs prod DB read for an incident.
Reasoning: Chatops request → auto-approval (on-call, incident channel) → 2h grant, read-only, session logged → auto-revoke. Total friction: 2 minutes.
Takeaway: JIT must be FASTER than the workaround, or users bypass it.
example.walkthrough: Map one standing-privilege workflow to a JIT design; prototype it.

pitfalls: JIT slower than asking a friend: friction drives circumvention.
Approval theater: auto-approve everything = standing access with paperwork.
No revocation testing: grants that do not expire are standing privilege.
lessons.try_it: Measure your JIT request-to-grant time; target under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Continuous Verification: Building the Loop
concepts: The loop: collect signals (identity, device, behavior) → evaluate per session → enforce at PEPs → log decisions → feed back into detection and policy tuning.
Session lifetimes by risk: 15 min for admin consoles, hours for standard apps, with re-verification triggers (posture change, anomaly, new location).
Revocation propagation: the kill chain (disable user → sessions die) must be TESTED and measured. Untested revocation is assumed, not verified.
Behavioral triggers: impossible travel, unusual volume, new device — each maps to step-up or terminate. Define the mapping; do not improvise during incidents.

example.code:
Worked example — the revoked session
Setup: Disable a test user at 14:00.
Reasoning: Measure: IdP sessions? App sessions? VPN? Record each kill latency. The slowest is your real revocation time.
Takeaway: The loop is only as fast as its slowest revocation.
example.walkthrough: Test revocation latency for your top 3 apps; document the slowest.

pitfalls: Login-only verification: the 8-hour trust window.
Untested kill chain: discovered during the incident.
Uniform session lifetimes: calibrate to risk.
lessons.try_it: Build the verification-loop diagram for one app, end to end.

lessons.title: Hardening Active Directory for Zero Trust
concepts: AD is the identity plane for most Windows shops — its compromise is total compromise. Tiered admin model (Tier 0/1/2), no DA logons to workstations, Protected Users for privileged accounts.

Concretely: dedicated Tier 0 admin workstations (hardened, no internet/email), separate admin accounts per tier, LAPS for local admins, authentication policies/silos limiting where privileged creds can be used.
Monitor: DC replication health, privileged group membership changes (alert on ANY), DCSync/DCShadow attempts (the classic AD attacks), Kerberos anomalies (golden/silver ticket indicators).
AD is not going away in most zero trust migrations — so it gets hardened as the identity foundation, with cloud IdP federated for modern auth. Both, defended.

example.code:
Worked example — the tier check
Setup: Audit: does any DA account log on to a workstation daily?
Reasoning: Check the logs. If yes: credential theft waiting to happen — move that admin to a Tier 2 account for daily work, Tier 0 only on the admin workstation.
Takeaway: Tier violations are the AD attack path.
example.walkthrough: Audit tier violations this week: privileged logons to lower tiers.

pitfalls: DA for daily work: every workstation compromise becomes forest compromise.
No LAPS: one local admin password everywhere = lateral movement kit.
Unmonitored DA group changes: the quietest privilege escalation.
lessons.try_it: Implement LAPS and the tier model; alert on violations.

lessons.title: Kerberos Hardening: Killing the Ticket Attacks
concepts: The attacks: golden ticket (KRBTGT hash → forge any ticket), silver ticket (service account hash → forge service tickets), Kerberoasting (request service tickets, crack offline), AS-REP roasting (no pre-auth accounts).

Defenses: KRBTGT double-reset (twice, 10h apart — invalidates goldens), strong service-account passwords (25+ chars, managed — kills roasting economics), pre-auth required everywhere, AES-only where possible (disable RC4).
Detection: anomalous ticket lifetimes/encryption types, SPN scanning, mass TGS requests (roasting telemetry), honeypot SPNs (a fake SPN whose ticket request = alert).
The meta-defense: tiering + credential hygiene shrinks what attackers can steal to forge with. Kerberos attacks need hashes; hashes come from compromised hosts.

example.code:
klist sessions | findstr /i 'aes'
# check your ticket encryption types — RC4 anywhere is a finding
example.walkthrough: Audit Kerberos encryption types in your domain; plan the RC4 disable.

pitfalls: Service accounts with weak passwords: Kerberoastable by design.
KRBTGT never reset: a golden ticket from 2019 still works.
No pre-auth on accounts: AS-REP roastable without any credential.
lessons.try_it: Reset KRBTGT twice; rotate the top 5 service-account passwords to 25+ chars.

lessons.title: AD Deception: Honeypots and Canaries
concepts: Deception turns the attacker's reconnaissance against them: honeypot accounts (fake admins that alert on any use), honeypot SPNs (fake services whose tickets are never legitimately requested), canary files/shares.
Implementation: create the decoys, ensure NOTHING legitimate touches them (baseline first), alert on ANY interaction. Any touch = compromise in progress, high fidelity.
AD-specific: fake DA accounts (named plausibly, e.g., 'svc-backup-admin'), fake SPNs on the honeypot, adminSDHolder-protected so they look real. Monitor 4768/4769 (ticket requests) for them.
Deception is detection, not prevention — it buys the one thing breaches lack: early, high-confidence warning. Deploy alongside, not instead of, hardening.

example.code:
Worked example — the honeypot DA
Setup: Create 'adm-backup02' (fake DA), no legitimate use.
Reasoning: Alert on any logon/ticket request for it. Attacker enumerating DAs tries it — you know in seconds, before damage.
Takeaway: The attacker's recon becomes your alarm.
example.walkthrough: Deploy one honeypot account and one canary file this week.

pitfalls: Honeypots that legitimate processes touch: baseline first, or alerts are noise.
Deception as the only detection: it is a tripwire, not a wall.
Obvious fakes ('honeypot-admin'): attackers ignore what looks planted.
lessons.try_it: Name decoys plausibly; verify zero legitimate touches for a week.

lessons.title: Identity Attack Path Mapping
concepts: Attack path analysis: from any compromised workstation, which paths lead to DA? Tools (BloodHound/SharpHound) map it — the graph usually shows 3-hop paths nobody suspected.
The fix loop: find shortest paths → break them (remove the ACL, the group nesting, the session) → re-run → repeat. Each iteration lengthens the attacker's path.
Common findings: users with DCSync rights (via nested groups), unconstrained delegation, AdminSDHolder misconfigurations, stale sessions on servers.
Run it regularly: the graph changes with every permission change. Monthly collection, quarterly remediation sprints. The graph is the AD security scorecard.

example.code:
.
SharpHound.exe -c All
# import to BloodHound, query: shortest path from 'Domain Users' to 'Domain Admins'
example.walkthrough: Run SharpHound in lab; find the shortest path to DA; break one link.

pitfalls: Running it once: the graph rots within weeks.
Collecting without remediating: the map of vulnerabilities, framed.
Breaking paths without testing: some 'links' are load-bearing — verify.
lessons.try_it: Schedule monthly collection; remediate the top 3 paths quarterly.

lessons.title: Host Firewall as the First Segment
concepts: The host firewall is microsegmentation's cheapest, finest unit: per-machine, identity-aware (with IPsec/auth), centrally managed, and it travels with the workload (VMs, cloud, laptops).
Implementation: GPO/Intune for Windows (default inbound block, explicit allows per role), Ansible/Puppet for Linux (nftables), cloud security groups for cloud. One policy source per platform.
Rule hygiene: every allow has owner + reason + expiry; default-deny inbound; log denies (the deny log is reconnaissance telemetry).
Start here because: no network changes needed, no outage risk when done in monitor-mode first, and it immediately shrinks every host's attack surface.

example.code:
Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Public,Private -DefaultInboundAction Block
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Allow RDP from admin subnet' -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 3389 -RemoteAddress 10.10.0.0/24 -Action Allow
example.walkthrough: Enable default-deny on a lab host; allow only what it needs; test.

pitfalls: Firewall off 'temporarily': the temporary that outlives the admin.
Allows without owners: the rule archaeology problem.
No central management: 500 hand-configured firewalls drift immediately.
lessons.try_it: Centrally manage host firewalls for one server tier this month.

lessons.title: Tier Segmentation in Practice
concepts: The classic three tiers: web (internet-facing, least trusted), app (middle, talks to web and data only), data (most trusted, talks to app tier only on DB ports). Plus management (admin-only) and DMZ/edge as needed.
Implement with: VLANs + firewall rules between them (on-prem), security groups + NACLs (cloud), host firewalls as the inner layer. Defense in depth, not one mechanism.

Traffic rules per tier (examples): web→app: HTTPS only, app servers' IPs; app→data: DB port only, from app SG; data→internet: deny (except patch/backup via proxy); management: admin workstations only.
Validate: from each tier, attempt to reach what should be denied — the test is the control. Untested segmentation is a diagram.

example.code:
Worked example — the DB tier test
Setup: From a web-tier host, try the DB port.
Reasoning: Blocked (correct). From app-tier: allowed (correct). From management: allowed for admin ports only. Three tests, three expected results.
Takeaway: Test every boundary from both sides.
example.walkthrough: Test every tier boundary in your lab; record pass/fail.

pitfalls: Tiers on paper, flat in practice: the diagram is not the control.
App tier with internet access 'for updates': proxy it, do not allow it.
No management tier: admin interfaces on user segments.
lessons.try_it: Build the tier matrix: source tier x dest tier x allowed ports.

lessons.title: Cloud Segmentation: VPCs and Security Groups
concepts: Cloud primitives: VPCs (the big boundary), subnets (public/private/database tiers), security groups (stateful, instance-level firewall), NACLs (stateless, subnet-level).

Patterns: public subnets (load balancers only), private subnets (apps, no public IPs), data subnets (databases, no internet route). Security groups reference EACH OTHER (app SG allows DB SG — not IP ranges).
SG hygiene = firewall hygiene: owner + reason + expiry per rule, no 0.0.0.0/0 to sensitive ports (alert on it), regular reviews. SGs as code (Terraform) with PR review.
Multi-account: separate accounts per environment/workload (the strongest cloud boundary) — segmentation at the account level beats any SG rule.

example.walkthrough: Audit your SGs for 0.0.0.0/0 to sensitive ports; remove or justify each.

pitfalls: 0.0.0.0/0 'temporary' rules: the cloud's commonest exposure.
SGs by IP instead of by SG reference: brittle, drift-prone.
One account for everything: the blast radius is the whole cloud bill.

lessons.title: Validating Segmentation: The Adversary Test
concepts: Segmentation is validated adversarially: from a compromised position, attempt what should be denied. The tester's mindset, applied to your own controls.
Test battery: (1) port-scan across tiers from each tier, (2) attempt lateral protocols (SMB/RDP/WinRM/SSH) cross-tier, (3) DNS exfiltration attempt, (4) verify deny logs recorded each attempt.
Automate: run the battery monthly (or on every firewall change). Segmentation decays — rules accrete, exceptions fossilize. The test catches the decay.
Red-team lite: give a junior admin a 'compromised' VM and 2 hours. What they reach is your real segmentation posture, not the diagram.

example.code:
# from web tier: what CAN you reach?
Test-NetConnection db01 -Port 1433   # expect: fail
Test-NetConnection app01 -Port 443  # expect: succeed
example.walkthrough: Run the adversary battery from each tier; fix what should have been denied.

pitfalls: Testing from the admin workstation: the most trusted position tells you nothing.
One-time test: segmentation rots; test on a cadence.
Ignoring the deny logs: the test should also validate DETECTION.
lessons.try_it: Automate the monthly segmentation test; trend the results.

lessons.title: TLS Everywhere: The Internal Mandate
concepts: Tenet: all communication secured, including 'internal.' Inventory every plaintext protocol (HTTP, LDAP, telnet, FTP, SNMPv1/2, SMB1) and eliminate or justify each.
mTLS for service-to-service: mutual authentication, not just server-side. The client proves identity too — this is workload identity in cryptographic form.
Certificate lifecycle for internal TLS: internal CA (AD CS or Vault PKI), auto-enrollment, monitored expiry, tested renewal. Internal certs expire too — plan like it.
Verify with captures: the packet capture is the proof. 'We enabled TLS' + a capture showing plaintext = not enabled. Trust, then verify, with Wireshark.

example.code:
# find plaintext LDAP
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'ldap' 2>/dev/null | head -5
# any hits = plaintext LDAP in use
example.walkthrough: Capture internal traffic; enumerate every plaintext protocol; remediate one.

pitfalls: 'Internal' exemption: the tenet has no such clause.
TLS enabled but not verified: the capture is the control.
Expired internal certs: the outage nobody monitors.
lessons.try_it: Run the plaintext hunt quarterly; drive the count to zero.

lessons.title: PKI Operations: Running Your Own CA
concepts: CA hierarchy: offline root (air-gapped, long life) → online intermediates (issuing CAs per purpose: servers, users, devices). Compromise of an intermediate costs re-issuance, not the root.
AD CS or Vault PKI: AD CS integrates with Windows auto-enrollment beautifully; Vault PKI suits dynamic/cloud workloads. Choose by ecosystem, operate deliberately either way.

Operations: CRL/OCSP publishing (revocation must be checkable), key ceremonies documented, CA backup (the CA's keys backed up securely — losing the CA key is losing the trust anchor), annual key-ceremony rehearsal.
The most neglected part: revocation. Issuance gets attention; CRL distribution, OCSP responder uptime, and client revocation CHECKING are where PKI actually fails.

example.code:
Worked example — the revocation test
Setup: Revoke a test cert.
Reasoning: Check: does the CRL update? Does OCSP respond? Does the CLIENT actually check? All three must be yes.
Takeaway: Revocation is a chain; test every link.
example.walkthrough: Revoke a test cert; verify CRL, OCSP, and client behavior.

pitfalls: Single-tier CA (root issuing directly): the crown jewels doing daily work.
No tested revocation: the compromise response is theoretical.
CA keys unbacked-up: the fire takes the trust anchor.
lessons.try_it: Document your CA hierarchy, CRL/OCSP endpoints, and the compromise runbook.

lessons.title: Secrets Management for Implementers
concepts: The rule: no human-known, long-lived secrets in code, config, or wikis. Every secret gets: a vault, an identity-based accessor, automatic rotation, and audit.
Patterns: app secrets → vault with dynamic credentials (or short-lived static with rotation); CI/CD secrets → OIDC-federated (no stored cloud keys); human break-glass → PAM-vaulted with checkout.
Rotation: automate it (the vault rotates; the app re-reads). Manual rotation does not happen — the 4-year-old password proves it.
Detection: scan repos and configs for secrets (gitleaks, trufflehog) in CI — committed secrets get revoked, not just deleted (git history remembers).

example.code:
# CI without stored keys: OIDC federation
# the pipeline mints short-lived cloud creds via identity, no static key
example.walkthrough: Scan one repo for secrets; rotate anything found; add the scanner to CI.

pitfalls: 'Temporary' secret in the config: the 4-year temporary.
Deleting the committed secret without rotating: history still has it.
Vault deployed but apps still use config files: the migration never finished.
lessons.try_it: Inventory every static secret; assign each a vault-migration date.

lessons.title: Crypto Agility: Ready for the Next Algorithm
concepts: Crypto agility: the ability to change algorithms without rebuilding systems — abstracted crypto libraries, configurable cipher suites, certificate agility (re-issue with new algorithms).
Why now: post-quantum transition is coming (NIST PQC standards published); algorithms deprecate (SHA-1, 3DES, TLS 1.0/1.1 behind us). The next deprecation will not ask permission.
Inventory: where is each algorithm used? (TLS configs, certificate signatures, disk encryption, code signing.) You cannot migrate what you have not inventoried.
Hybrid deployments: during transitions, support old+new simultaneously (hybrid certs, negotiated suites), then remove the old. The transition is a project; start the inventory now.

example.code:
nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 internal-app.local
# inventory what the app actually negotiates
example.walkthrough: Inventory cipher suites on your top 10 internal services.

pitfalls: Hardcoded algorithms: the migration requires code changes per instance.
No inventory: the deprecation notice arrives as a surprise.
'Quantum is far away': the transition takes YEARS; start the inventory now.
lessons.try_it: Build the algorithm inventory; flag anything already deprecated.

lessons.title: Application Allowlisting: Implementation
concepts: Allowlisting (AppLocker/WDAC): only approved executables run. The default-deny for code execution — malware that cannot execute cannot infect.
AppLocker (GPO-managed, simpler): publisher rules (signed by vendor X), path rules, hash rules. Start in AUDIT mode: collect what WOULD be blocked, tune, then enforce.
WDAC (stronger, harder): code-integrity policies, kernel-enforced, managed via policy XML. For high-security endpoints (admin workstations, servers).
Rollout: audit → tune (the business apps you forgot) → enforce per OU → monitor bypass attempts (blocked executions are threat intel). Never enforce day one.

example.code:
Worked example — the audit phase
Setup: AppLocker audit mode on pilot OU for 2 weeks.
Reasoning: Review the would-block list: the line-of-business app from System32\oddpath, the updater, the admin's tools. Allowlist them deliberately, THEN enforce.
Takeaway: Audit mode is discovery; enforcement is the decision.
example.walkthrough: Enable AppLocker audit mode on a pilot OU; review the would-blocks.

pitfalls: Enforce day one: the business stops, and allowlisting gets blamed forever.
Path rules for user-writable dirs: the classic bypass (write malware to the allowed path).
No bypass-attempt monitoring: blocked executions are free threat intel.
lessons.try_it: Tune the audit data; enforce on the pilot OU next month.

lessons.title: Allowlisting Bypass Techniques (Red Team)
concepts: Know the bypasses to defend: LOLBins (living-off-the-land binaries — signed Microsoft tools abused: mshta, rundll32, regsvr32), path-rule abuse (writable allowed paths), DLL hijacking, macro/script interpreters (allowlisted python.exe running evil.py).

Defense per bypass: publisher rules over path rules (signed code, not locations), block/constrain LOLBins via policy (or EDR rules), script enforcement (Constrained Language Mode + script allowlisting), DLL rules where feasible.
Test your policy: run the common bypasses in lab against your ruleset. The bypass that works is your next rule.
Allowlisting is one layer: pair with EDR (behavioral) and least privilege. No single control survives contact with a creative attacker.

example.code:
# test: can you run this?
rundll32.exe javascript:'\..\mshtml,RunHTMLApplication';alert('test')
# if it runs, your policy has a LOLBin hole
example.walkthrough: Test 5 common LOLBins against your (audit-mode) policy; record results.

pitfalls: Publisher rules with '*': the vendor's cert allows ANY of their binaries, including the abusable ones.
Ignoring scripts: 'applications' allowlisted, PowerShell wide open.
Set-and-forget: new LOLBins emerge; review bypass lists yearly.
lessons.try_it: Block or constrain the LOLBins your testing found.

lessons.title: Script and Macro Controls
concepts: Scripts are code: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + WDAC/Applocker script rules, macro policies (block internet macros — the #1 initial access vector), signed-scripts-only where feasible.
Office macros: the historic king of initial access. Policy: block macros from the internet (Mark of the Web), allow only signed/trusted-location macros, and even those get scrutiny.
PowerShell: Constrained Language Mode via WDAC/Applocker breaks most offensive tradecraft (no Add-Type, no arbitrary .NET). Pair with script-block logging + AMSI for visibility.
HTA/JS/VBS: constrain or block the interpreters themselves where the business allows. Each interpreter is an execution path allowlisting must cover.

example.code:
# check language mode
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode
# ConstrainedLanguage on locked-down hosts
example.walkthrough: Check language mode on your hosts; enable Constrained via WDAC on admins' workstations.

pitfalls: Allowlisting EXEs but ignoring scripts: the attacker just changes file extensions.
Internet macros allowed: the phishing attachment runs on open.
No script-block logging: the constrained bypasses go unseen.
lessons.try_it: Block internet macros via GPO; verify with a test document.

lessons.title: Maintaining the Allowlist: Change Control
concepts: The allowlist is a living control: new apps, updates (new hashes/versions), vendor cert changes — each needs a governed path (request → review → test → approve → deploy).
Publisher rules age well (vendor cert covers updates); hash rules rot fast (every update breaks). Prefer publisher > path (carefully) > hash. Design for the update cycle.
Emergency path: the 2 AM legitimate-block needs a fast allow (with retroactive review). If the emergency path is slower than disabling enforcement, users will disable enforcement.
Metrics: block rate, false-positive rate, time-to-allow for legit requests. The allowlist's health is measured, not assumed.

example.code:
Worked example — the update Tuesday
Setup: Vendor ships update; hash rules break; 200 users blocked.
Reasoning: With publisher rules: nothing breaks (same cert). With hash rules: fire drill. The rule TYPE determines operational cost.
Takeaway: Choose rule types for the update reality.
example.walkthrough: Audit your rule types: what breaks on the next vendor update?

pitfalls: Hash-only rules: every Patch Tuesday is an incident.
No emergency allow path: the control gets disabled 'temporarily.'
Unmeasured false positives: the business quietly hates the control.
lessons.try_it: Convert hash rules to publisher rules where the vendor signs consistently.

lessons.title: Purple Teaming: The Collaborative Exercise
concepts: Purple team: red and blue work TOGETHER — red executes an attack step, blue shows what they saw (or missed), both tune. It is a training and tuning exercise, not a competition.
Format: pick ONE technique (e.g., Kerberoasting) → red executes → blue hunts live → debrief: what fired, what did not, what to tune. One technique per session, deep.
Output: tuned detections, new alerts, fixed gaps — measured (detection time before/after). The exercise's value is the DELTA, not the theater.
Cadence: monthly technique sessions beat annual mega-exercises. Small, frequent, cumulative.

example.code:
Worked example — the Kerberoasting session
Setup: Red requests service tickets en masse.
Reasoning: Blue: did the TGS-storm alert fire? (No → write it.) Did the honeypot SPN trip? (Yes → good.) Tune, re-run, measure.
Takeaway: One technique, fully instrumented, then move on.
example.walkthrough: Run one purple-team session on a single technique this month.

pitfalls: Red vs blue scorekeeping: competition kills collaboration.
Annual mega-exercise only: too rare to build muscle.
No measured delta: the exercise was entertainment.
lessons.try_it: Schedule monthly technique sessions; track detection deltas.

lessons.title: Detection Engineering: From Technique to Alert
concepts: Detection engineering: for each adversary technique (MITRE ATT&CK), define: data source, detection logic, tuning, response playbook. Detections are built, not bought.
Process: pick a technique relevant to your threats → verify the logs exist → write the rule → test with an atomic (Atomic Red Team) → tune false positives → document + assign.
Atomic testing: run the technique safely in lab, confirm the alert fires, confirm the benign baseline does NOT fire it. Both directions matter.
Coverage map: track which ATT&CK techniques have detections, which are missing. The map prioritizes the next engineering sprint.

example.code:
# atomic test example (Atomic Red Team)
Invoke-AtomicTest T1558.003 -ShowDetailsBrief
# Kerberoasting: does YOUR detection fire?
example.walkthrough: Pick one technique; verify log source; write the detection; atomic-test it.

pitfalls: Vendor-default rules only: generic coverage, your-specific gaps.
Detections never tested: the rule that never fires (broken) or always fires (noise).
No coverage map: engineering by gut feel.
lessons.try_it: Build the ATT&CK coverage map for your top 20 techniques.

lessons.title: Threat Hunting: Hypothesis-Driven
concepts: Hunting: proactive searching for undetected compromise — hypothesis ('Kerberoasting happened here') → data → analysis → conclusion (found / not found / inconclusive + new hypothesis).
Hypotheses come from: threat intel (sector-targeted techniques), red-team findings (paths that worked), and crown-jewel analysis (how WOULD they reach it?).
Timebox: 1–2 week sprints per hypothesis. Document everything — negative results are valuable (they validate the detections).
Hunting feeds engineering: every hunt that finds a gap produces a detection. Hunts without detection output are expensive curiosity.

example.code:
Worked example — the hunt
Setup: Hypothesis: 'An attacker Kerberoasted us last quarter.'
Reasoning: Pull TGS request logs → look for volume anomalies + honeypot SPN hits → found: 3 anomalous bursts in March → investigate → new detection for the pattern.
Takeaway: Hypothesis in, detection out.
example.walkthrough: Run one hunt this quarter; produce one detection from it.

pitfalls: Hunting without hypotheses: log-diving as a hobby.
No timebox: the 6-month hunt that never concludes.
Findings without detections: the next hunter re-finds it.
lessons.try_it: Write 3 hunt hypotheses from your threat intel; prioritize one.

lessons.title: Adversary Emulation: Full-Cycle Exercises
concepts: Adversary emulation: replicate a REAL threat actor's full kill chain (e.g., ransomware affiliate: phish → persist → escalate → move laterally → exfiltrate/encrypt) against your environment, safely.
Plan: intelligence (which actor, their TTPs), scoping (what is in/out of bounds — safety), execution (phased, with blue team partially blind), debrief (timeline vs detections).
Measure the kill chain: where did they get stopped (or not)? Each un-stopped phase is a program gap with a name. The report reads as phases, not findings.
Follow-through: every un-stopped phase gets a remediation owner and a re-test date. Emulation without remediation is an expensive story.

example.code:
Worked example — the ransomware emulation
Setup: Emulate affiliate TTPs through encryption (stopped before actual encryption).
Reasoning: Phish: caught by training. Persist: caught by EDR. Lateral: NOT caught (flat segment) → finding with owner. Exfil: caught by DLP.
Takeaway: The un-stopped phase is the roadmap.
example.walkthrough: Plan one emulation for next quarter; define the stop-conditions.

pitfalls: Emulation as pentest: it is TTP-replication, not vulnerability scanning.
No safety scoping: the emulation becomes the incident.
Report without phase-mapped remediation: findings without owners.
lessons.try_it: Choose the actor to emulate based on your sector's threats.

lessons.title: EDR as a Zero Trust Signal Source
concepts: EDR telemetry maps to trust signals: agent installed/running (presence), definitions current (hygiene), active detections (compromise state), isolation state (containment). Each maps to a device-trust input.

Integration architecture: EDR console/API → device compliance engine or SIEM → policy engine (conditional access / NAC). Define the data flow, the freshness SLA, and the failure mode (EDR down = fail closed or open? decide explicitly).
Signal mapping table: EDR 'healthy' → compliant; 'detections active' → non-compliant + step-up; 'isolated' → untrusted, kill sessions; 'not reporting' → unknown → untrusted (fail closed).
Test the mapping: each state transition tested end to end (infect a lab VM → watch the access decision change). Untested mappings are assumptions.

example.code:
Worked example — the signal table
Setup: EDR states mapped to CA device conditions.
Reasoning: Test: lab VM gets EICAR → EDR flags → compliance flips → CA blocks new sessions → existing sessions revoked. Measure each hop's latency.
Takeaway: The table is the contract; the test proves it.
example.walkthrough: Write your EDR-to-trust signal mapping table; test one transition.

pitfalls: EDR deployed but not wired: detection without access impact.
'Not reporting' = neutral: the attacker's first move is killing the agent.
No freshness SLA: yesterday's 'healthy' deciding today's access.
lessons.try_it: Define the fail-closed/fail-open decision for EDR outage, in writing.

lessons.title: Automated Response: Isolation to Revocation
concepts: The response chain: EDR detects → isolates the host (network quarantine) → signals the identity plane → sessions revoked → SOC notified → ticket created. Each hop automated, each hop logged.
Isolation first: network quarantine stops lateral movement in seconds — faster than any human. But isolation must not strand the SOC's own access (out-of-band management path).
Session revocation: the EDR signal must reach the IdP/CA to kill cloud/app sessions — host isolation alone leaves the attacker's stolen sessions alive elsewhere.
Playbook the exceptions: what does NOT auto-isolate (domain controllers? the CEO's laptop during the board meeting?) — define, document, and require human approval for those.

example.code:
Worked example — the ransomware host
Setup: EDR flags ransomware behavior.
Reasoning: Auto: isolate host (3s) → revoke user sessions (30s) → SOC paged with context → analyst confirms, starts IR. Human time spent on judgment, not mechanics.
Takeaway: Automate the mechanics; reserve humans for decisions.
example.walkthrough: Map your response chain hop by hop; measure each hop's latency in lab.

pitfalls: Isolation without session revocation: the host is quarantined, the stolen cloud sessions live on.
Auto-isolating DCs: the cure worse than the disease — exception-list critical infra.
No out-of-band path: the SOC cannot reach the isolated host to investigate.
lessons.try_it: Define the auto-isolation exception list with justifications.

lessons.title: EDR Tuning: Fidelity Over Volume
concepts: Alert fidelity is the metric: true-positive rate per rule, tuned until analysts trust the alerts. Untuned EDR trains bulk-closing — real attacks hide in the noise analysts ignore.

Tuning process: baseline (what fires normally?), suppress the benign (known-good admin tools, with scoping — not blanket exclusions), escalate the rare-and-dangerous (credential dumping, LSASS access, DCSync).
Exclusions are risk acceptances: every exclusion gets owner + reason + expiry + review. Blanket path exclusions ('exclude C:\Tools\*') are attacker real estate.
Measure: alerts per analyst per day (target: single digits of real work), MTTD trend, and the 'would we have caught last year's incident' retro-test.

example.code:
Worked example — the noisy rule
Setup: Rule fires 500x/day on the admin's scripts.
Reasoning: Tune: scope the exclusion to the script's hash + the admin's host (not '*'), keep the rule live for everything else. Volume drops 95%, coverage kept.
Takeaway: Precision exclusions, not blanket ones.
example.walkthrough: Pick your noisiest EDR rule; precision-tune it this week.

pitfalls: Bulk-closing alerts: the culture that misses the real one.
Blanket exclusions: the attacker's allowlist.
Tuning once: the environment changes; tuning is continuous.
lessons.try_it: Set the quarterly EDR tuning review with fidelity metrics.

lessons.title: EDR Coverage Gaps: Servers, Linux, Cloud
concepts: Coverage inventory: every endpoint class — Windows workstations AND servers, Linux, macOS, cloud VMs, containers. The gap is always where you did not look (servers 'too critical,' Linux 'does not get malware').

Servers: EDR on servers with server-tuned policies (different baselines — servers do weird-but-legitimate things). 'Too critical for agents' is 2010 thinking; modern agents are safe, and unmonitored servers are the lateral-movement highway.
Cloud/container: workload EDR or eBPF-based runtime security for containers; cloud VM agents via the same console. Ephemeral workloads need API-driven coverage (auto-enroll on spin-up).
Measure coverage: % of each class with healthy agents, reported weekly. The uncovered percentage is the attacker's address space.

example.code:
Worked example — the server gap
Setup: EDR on 100% of workstations, 40% of servers.
Reasoning: The red team lives on the unmonitored 60% of servers. Close it: server-tuned policy, phased rollout, coverage metric to 95%+.
Takeaway: Attackers go where the EDR is not.
example.walkthrough: Inventory EDR coverage by endpoint class; close the biggest gap first.

pitfalls: Workstations-only EDR: the server blind spot.
One policy for all: server baselines differ — tune per class.
Ephemeral cloud VMs without auto-enrollment: the 4-hour-lived attacker host.
lessons.try_it: Publish the weekly coverage percentage per class.

lessons.title: CA Policy Anatomy
concepts: Every CA policy: ASSIGNMENTS (who: users/groups; what: apps — target precisely), CONDITIONS (signals: device, location, risk, client app), ACCESS CONTROLS (grant: require MFA / compliant device / block; session: limits, app-enforced restrictions).

Evaluation: all enabled policies evaluate; the MOST restrictive outcome wins for blocks, and grants combine (require MFA AND compliant device if both policies demand). Order matters less than completeness — but know YOUR platform's logic.
Design pattern: baseline policies first (require MFA for all users; block legacy auth; require compliant devices for sensitive apps), then app-tier policies, then exceptions (named, owned, expiring).
Report-only mode: every new policy runs in report-only first — review what WOULD happen, tune, then enforce. 'Enforce and see who complains' is an outage generator.

example.code:
Worked example — the baseline trio
Setup: Three policies: (1) all users, all apps: require MFA. (2) all users: block legacy auth protocols. (3) finance app: require compliant device + MFA.
Reasoning: Baseline coverage in 3 policies; report-only for a week; enforce.
Takeaway: Baselines first, tiers second, exceptions last.
example.walkthrough: Draft your baseline trio; run in report-only; review the would-dos.

pitfalls: One mega-policy: unreadable, untestable, undebuggable.
Enforce-first: the helpdesk learns about the policy from the tickets.
No legacy-auth block: the MFA bypass sitting in plain sight.
lessons.try_it: Block legacy authentication this month — it is the MFA bypass.

lessons.title: Conditions: Signals That Drive Decisions
concepts: Signal inventory: device compliance/state, location (named locations, GPS for mobile), risk (user risk, sign-in risk from identity protection), client app (browser vs legacy), device platform, insider-risk indicators.
Signal quality: conditions are only as good as their inputs — stale device compliance, unmaintained named locations, and unreviewed risk policies produce wrong decisions confidently.
Location reality: IP-based location is approximate (VPNs, CGNAT, travel). Use it for step-up, not for hard blocks — unless paired with stronger signals.

Risk-based: user/sign-in risk from the identity protection engine — unfamiliar location + anonymous IP + leaked credentials = high risk → block or require password change. Wire risk into the grant controls.

example.code:
Worked example — the risky sign-in
Setup: Sign-in risk = high (leaked creds + Tor exit).
Reasoning: Policy: high user risk → require password change + block until remediated. The automation contains the compromised credential.
Takeaway: Risk signals turn detection into prevention.
example.walkthrough: Audit your named locations and risk policies for staleness this quarter.

pitfalls: IP-location hard blocks: the traveling executive locked out, the attacker on residential IP allowed.
Risk policies never reviewed: the 'medium risk' threshold from 2020.
Conditions without signal hygiene: garbage in, locked-out users.
lessons.try_it: Define the signal-freshness SLA per condition type.

lessons.title: Grant Controls and Session Controls
concepts: Grant controls: what the user must satisfy — require MFA, require compliant/hybrid-joined device, require approved app, block. Combine with AND (all required) across policies; understand OR within.

Session controls: limit AFTER access — sign-in frequency (re-auth interval), app-enforced restrictions (Exchange/SharePoint limited experience for unmanaged), Conditional Access App Control (CASB session proxy: block download, watermark).
Persistent browser session: balance UX and risk (persistent for managed, never for unmanaged). These small settings shape daily friction enormously.
Design rule: grant controls answer 'may they in?'; session controls answer 'what may they do inside?' Both calibrated by app sensitivity.

example.code:
Worked example — the unmanaged device
Setup: Personal laptop, needs email.
Reasoning: Grant: MFA (allowed). Session: app-enforced restrictions — web-only Outlook, no download, 1h sign-in frequency. The device never holds the data.
Takeaway: Session controls make BYOD viable.
example.walkthrough: Design grant + session controls for your 3 app tiers.

pitfalls: Grant-only design: inside the app, anything goes.
Uniform session controls: the wiki and the ERP deserve different sessions.
No app-enforced restrictions: unmanaged devices downloading everything.
lessons.try_it: Pilot session controls on one app; measure friction vs risk.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting CA: The Sign-In Log
concepts: The sign-in log is the CA debugger: every authentication shows which policies applied, which conditions matched, and the exact failure (policy name + unmet control). Start EVERY CA investigation here.

Methodology: find the user's sign-in → open the CA tab → read the policy evaluation (applied/not-applied per policy, with reasons) → identify the failing condition → fix the condition or the signal (not the policy's existence).
Common: 'device not compliant' (fix the device, not the policy), 'location not in named locations' (update locations or use step-up), 'legacy client blocked' (modernize the client).
Proactive: review report-only results weekly; alert on spikes in CA failures (attack or broken rollout — both urgent).

example.code:
Worked example — the blocked exec
Setup: Exec blocked from email, traveling.
Reasoning: Sign-in log → policy 'Sensitive apps: compliant device' → condition failed: device shows non-compliant (EDR definitions stale). Fix: update EDR, re-check compliance, access restored. 10 minutes, no policy change.
Takeaway: The log names the fix.
example.walkthrough: Diagnose 3 historical CA blocks using only the sign-in log.

pitfalls: Guessing: 'the policy is wrong' without reading the log.
Fixing the policy for a device problem: the next device breaks the same way.
No report-only review: the failures surprise you in production.
lessons.try_it: Write the CA triage runbook: log → policy → condition → fix.

lessons.title: PAM Architecture: Vaulting the Keys
concepts: Core pattern: privileged credentials live in the vault — humans never know them. Access = checkout (authenticated, approved, time-bound) → use (proxied/recorded) → check-in (auto-rotated).
Components: credential vault (the safe), access broker/proxy (the gate — sessions proxied, no direct creds), approval workflow, session recording, automatic rotation.
What goes in: domain admin, cloud root/IAM, network device enables, service accounts, database sysadmin, break-glass. If it is privileged and standing, it belongs in the vault.
The migration: discover (scan for privileged creds — scripts, wikis, configs), onboard (vault + rotate), cut over (break the old static creds), verify (old creds dead).

example.code:
Worked example — the onboarding
Setup: 5 DAs with known passwords in a spreadsheet.
Reasoning: Vault them → rotate each (spreadsheet copies die) → admins check out via PAM → spreadsheet shredded. Standing knowledge becomes standing ignorance (of the password) — by design.
Takeaway: The vaulting moment kills the spreadsheet.
example.walkthrough: Inventory privileged credentials; vault the top 5 this quarter.

pitfalls: Vault without rotation: the vault becomes a password museum.
Partial onboarding: the un-vaulted DA is the attacker's choice.
No proxy/record: checkout without session control is a library, not PAM.
lessons.try_it: Define 'privileged' for your org; inventory against the definition.

lessons.title: Just-in-Time Elevation in Practice
concepts: JIT flow: request (portal/chatops/ticket) → verify (MFA, business justification) → approve (manager/auto for standard, human for sensitive) → grant (time-bound, scoped) → revoke (automatic) → audit (who, what, when, why).
Ephemeral accounts option: instead of elevating a standing account, mint a temporary privileged account per request — it never existed before and ceases after. Maximum hygiene.
Approval design: standard requests (dev DB read, 2h) auto-approve with guardrails; sensitive (prod write, DA) require human approval. Calibrate friction to risk.
The UX imperative: JIT must be faster than the workaround. If checkout takes 30 minutes, admins share the standing cred 'just this once' — permanently. Target: minutes.

example.code:
Worked example — the 2-minute checkout
Setup: Admin needs prod server access.
Reasoning: Chatops '/pam request prod-web-03 2h incident-1234' → MFA push → auto-approved (incident channel, on-call) → proxied RDP, recorded → auto-revoke. 2 minutes, fully audited.
Takeaway: Speed is a security feature.
example.walkthrough: Prototype one JIT flow; time it; get it under 5 minutes.

pitfalls: 30-minute checkouts: the workaround wins.
Rubber-stamp approvals: standing access with paperwork.
No auto-revoke testing: the grant that lives forever.
lessons.try_it: Measure request-to-access time monthly; keep it under 5 min.

lessons.title: Session Recording and Monitoring
concepts: Record privileged sessions: video/text logs of everything done with elevated access — the audit trail and the forensic record. Proxy-based PAM records by construction.
Monitor live for the dangerous: alert on privileged sessions doing anomalous things (mass deletion, new account creation, data export) — recording without monitoring is a archive, not a control.
Review cadence: sample privileged sessions weekly (spot-check), review ALL break-glass sessions (mandatory), and feed session metadata to the SIEM (who elevated, where, what).
Privacy/legal: privileged users know sessions are recorded (policy + banner). The recording protects the admin too — 'I did not do that' is disprovable.

example.code:
Worked example — the 3 AM session
Setup: Alert: DA session at 3 AM creating accounts.
Reasoning: Recording shows: not the usual admin's patterns → compromised checkout? → kill session, rotate, investigate. The recording made the call in minutes.
Takeaway: Recorded sessions are investigable sessions.
example.walkthrough: Verify session recording works for one PAM path; review a sample.

pitfalls: Recording without review: the archive nobody opens.
No live alerting: the 3 AM account creation discovered Monday.
Unrecorded break-glass: the highest-privilege path, invisible.
lessons.try_it: Set the weekly privileged-session sampling review.

lessons.title: Service Account Governance via PAM
concepts: Service accounts in PAM: vaulted credentials, automatic rotation (the PAM rotates what humans cannot), usage monitoring (a service account doing interactive logons = alert), and ownership (every account has a human owner).
Discovery: scan for service accounts (scripts, scheduled tasks, app configs, wiki) — the shadow inventory is always bigger than the known one.
Rotation without breakage: PAM coordinates rotation with the consuming systems (staged rotation: new cred active, old valid during cutover, then old killed). Test in pre-prod first.
The end state: no human knows any service-account password; every account has an owner, a rotation schedule, and usage monitoring. Standing shared secrets: zero.

example.code:
Worked example — the wiki password
Setup: Service account password in the team wiki, 3 years old.
Reasoning: Vault it → rotate (wiki copy dies) → apps pull from vault/API → monitor usage → the wiki becomes documentation, not a credential store.
Takeaway: Every found password gets vaulted and rotated.
example.walkthrough: Find 5 service-account passwords outside the vault; onboard them.

pitfalls: Rotating without coordinating consumers: the Monday outage.
Orphan accounts (no owner): un-rotable, un-killable, un-auditable.
Human-known service passwords: the pattern PAM exists to kill.
lessons.try_it: Assign owners to every service account; no orphans by quarter-end.

lessons.title: Classification Scheme Design
concepts: Design the levels: typical 4 (Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted) with crisp definitions + EXAMPLES per level. 'Confidential: customer PII, e.g., SSNs, account numbers.' Examples prevent debates.

Handling rules per level: Restricted = encrypted + PAM access + no email + DLP block; Confidential = encrypted + role access + DLP monitor; Internal = standard controls; Public = no restrictions. Each level's rules are the operational payoff.
Keep it simple: 3–4 levels maximum. Ten levels = nobody classifies correctly. The scheme must fit on one page.
Ownership: data owners per domain (who decides 'restricted' for finance data?). Classification without owners is unmaintained the day after the workshop.

example.code:
Worked example — the one-pager
Setup: One page: 4 levels, definition + 3 examples + handling rules each.
Reasoning: If it does not fit on one page, it will not be used. Print it; it becomes the desk reference.
Takeaway: Simplicity is the adoption strategy.
example.walkthrough: Draft the one-page scheme with examples; socialize it this month.

pitfalls: 10-level schemes: precision nobody uses.
Definitions without examples: every team interprets differently.
No handling rules: labels that change nothing.
lessons.try_it: Get executive sign-off on the scheme — it needs authority.

lessons.title: Labeling: Making Classification Stick
concepts: Labels must be machine-readable to be enforceable: sensitivity labels (MIP) on documents/emails, column tags in databases, S3/object tags. Human-readable headers help; machine labels enforce.
Auto-labeling: DLP/policy engines label by content (SSN patterns → Confidential) — scales beyond manual labeling. Manual labeling for the crown jewels; auto for the long tail.

Label-driven enforcement: DLP reads labels (Restricted → block external sharing), access policies read labels (Restricted DB columns → PAM only), retention reads labels. The label is the policy input.
User education: the 'why' behind labeling (one 30-min session + the one-pager). Users who understand label correctly; users who do not, do not.

example.code:
Worked example — the auto-label
Setup: DLP rule: SSN pattern in a document → auto-label Confidential + notify author.
Reasoning: The author learns the scheme by doing; the document gets protected automatically. Education + enforcement in one motion.
Takeaway: Auto-labeling teaches while it protects.
example.walkthrough: Pilot auto-labeling on one document library; measure accuracy.

pitfalls: Manual-only labeling: covers 5% of the data, abandons the rest.
Labels nothing reads: decoration, not control.
No user education: mislabeled everything, confidently.
lessons.try_it: Connect one enforcement (DLP/retention) to labels this quarter.

lessons.title: Handling Rules per Level
concepts: Restricted: encryption at rest + in transit, PAM-gated access with justification, no external sharing (DLP block), watermarking, full audit. The crown-jewel protocol.
Confidential: encryption, role-based access, DLP monitor (alert, allow with justification), no personal-device storage.
Internal: standard access controls, DLP light monitoring, shareable within the company.
Public: no restrictions — but VERIFY it is actually public (the 'public' folder with the salary spreadsheet is the classic finding).

example.code:
Worked example — the salary spreadsheet
Setup: Found in 'Public' share.
Reasoning: Misclassified (should be Restricted/Confidential) → reclassify, restrict, investigate exposure (who accessed?), fix the process that put it there.
Takeaway: Audit the 'Public' label hardest — it is where misclassification hides.
example.walkthrough: Audit your 'Public' shares for misclassified data this month.

pitfalls: Handling rules nobody follows: the scheme is a poster.
Restricted without PAM: the label says crown jewel, the access says everyone.
No misclassification process: findings with no remediation path.
lessons.try_it: Write the misclassification remediation playbook (find → contain → reclassify → review).

lessons.title: Data Discovery and Inventory
concepts: You cannot classify what you have not found: discovery scans (file shares, databases, SaaS, endpoints) for sensitive patterns — the SSN in the marketing share, the keys in the repo, the PII in the analytics export.
Continuous, not one-time: new data arrives daily; discovery runs on a cadence (weekly scans, CI checks on code, DLP on egress). The inventory is a living artifact.
Prioritize by risk: crown-jewel systems first (customer DB, finance), then the long tail. Perfect inventory of everything is a multi-year project; inventoried crown jewels this quarter is a win.
The inventory feeds everything: DLP policies, access reviews, retention, breach-scope analysis. It is the data program's foundation document.

example.code:
# scan a share for SSN patterns (example)
Select-String -Path '\\share\dept\*' -Pattern '\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b' -Recurse 2>$null | Select Path, LineNumber
example.walkthrough: Scan one file share for sensitive patterns; triage the hits.

pitfalls: One-time discovery: the inventory rots within months.
Scanning without triage: 10,000 hits, zero actions.
Ignoring SaaS/endpoint: the data lives where the scan does not reach.
lessons.try_it: Schedule recurring discovery; assign triage ownership.

lessons.title: IR Under ZTA: What Changes
concepts: What ZTA gives IR: fast containment levers (kill user sessions, revoke device trust, isolate via EDR — all in minutes), rich telemetry (every access decision logged), and blast-radius limits (segmentation contains the breach).

What changes in the playbook: containment starts with IDENTITY and DEVICE (disable account, revoke sessions, quarantine device) — not with pulling network cables. The playbook's first 15 minutes are identity-plane actions.
What does NOT change: the IR phases (prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons-learned), evidence preservation, and communication discipline. ZTA upgrades the tools, not the methodology.
Prepare the levers BEFORE the incident: test session revocation, verify EDR isolation works, confirm the PAM break-glass path. Untested levers fail when pulled.

example.code:
Worked example — the first 15 minutes
Setup: Phished credential, active session.
Reasoning: Min 0–2: disable user, revoke sessions (IdP). Min 2–5: EDR isolate device. Min 5–15: scope (what did the session touch? — access logs), preserve evidence, notify. Contained before the coffee cools.
Takeaway: Identity-first containment, measured in minutes.
example.walkthrough: Tabletop the first-15-minutes with your actual tools; time each action.

pitfalls: Network-first containment thinking: the ZTA levers are identity/device.
Untested revocation: the lever that does not move.
No evidence preservation: containment that destroys the investigation.
lessons.try_it: Write the ZTA IR quick-reference card (one page, first 15 minutes).

lessons.title: Containment via Identity and Device
concepts: The containment toolkit: disable user (IdP), revoke sessions/tokens (IdP + app-level), revoke device trust (compliance flip → CA denies), EDR network isolation (host quarantine), rotate compromised credentials (service accounts, API keys).

Order matters: kill sessions BEFORE disabling the user? (Attacker with a valid session does not care about the password change.) Standard: revoke sessions + disable simultaneously via automation, then isolate the device.
Scope while containing: access logs show what the compromised identity touched — scope the blast radius from the telemetry (which is rich, because ZTA logs decisions).
Verify containment: re-check (is the session really dead? test it), monitor for re-entry (new sessions from the attacker = missed persistence).

example.code:
Worked example — the verification
Setup: Contained the phished account.
Reasoning: Verify: attempt the old session token (should fail), check for new sessions (none), check the device (isolated), rotate the creds it touched. Containment is not declared; it is VERIFIED.
Takeaway: Test the containment, do not assume it.
example.walkthrough: Build the containment checklist with verification steps per action.

pitfalls: Password reset without session revoke: the oldest mistake, still common.
Declaring containment without verifying: the attacker disagrees.
Forgetting service/API credentials: the user is contained, the API key is not.
lessons.try_it: Automate the containment sequence; the runbook triggers it in one action.

lessons.title: Eradication and Recovery in a ZTA World
concepts: Eradication: remove persistence (the ZTA telemetry shows everywhere the identity/device went — follow it), rotate ALL credentials the attacker touched (user, service, API keys — assume touched = compromised), rebuild compromised hosts from known-good (not 'cleaned').

Recovery order: identity plane first (clean IdP, re-verify admins), then trust signals (EDR healthy, compliance true), then restore access in tiers (critical users, then broad). Do not restore trust before verifying the plane.

The ZTA advantage in recovery: phased re-trust — users come back THROUGH the verification (MFA reset, device re-compliance), not around it. Recovery strengthens the posture instead of just restoring it.
Communicate: who was affected, what was accessed, what changed. The notification discipline is part of recovery, not an afterthought.

example.code:
Worked example — the phased return
Setup: 50 affected users, recovering.
Reasoning: Tier 1 (IT/admins): password reset + FIDO2 re-register + device re-image/re-verify. Tier 2: password reset + MFA re-verify. Each tier's return is a verification event.
Takeaway: Recovery through verification, not around it.
example.walkthrough: Write the tiered recovery sequence for a credential-compromise scenario.

pitfalls: 'Cleaned' hosts returned to service: rebuild, do not disinfect, for compromised hosts.
Restoring access before the plane is clean: re-compromise on schedule.
Skipping the touched-credential rotation: the attacker's spare keys.
lessons.try_it: Define 'known-good' for your host rebuilds (image source, verification).

lessons.title: Lessons Learned: The Post-Incident Engine
concepts: The post-mortem: blameless, timeline-driven (detection → containment → eradication → recovery, with timestamps), focused on systemic fixes (which CONTROL failed? which PROCESS?).
ZTA-specific questions: which signal failed (or was missing)? Did revocation propagate in time? Did segmentation contain as designed? Was the telemetry sufficient to scope?
Output: remediations with owners and dates (not 'improve monitoring' — 'deploy EDR-to-CA signal for Linux fleet by Q3, owner: X'), detection improvements, and playbook updates.
Track remediation like incidents: the post-mortem is not done when written; it is done when the remediations ship. Unshipped remediations are the next incident's preface.

example.code:
Worked example — the action items
Setup: Post-mortem of the phishing incident.
Reasoning: Bad: 'improve awareness.' Good: 'FIDO2 for finance team by Aug (owner: Y); EDR-isolation auto-revoke wired by Jul (owner: Z); CA policy: block non-compliant for ERP (done).' Named, dated, verifiable.
Takeaway: Remediations are deliverables, not sentiments.
example.walkthrough: Run a post-mortem on your last tabletop; write 3 named, dated remediations.

pitfalls: Blameful post-mortems: the next incident goes unreported.
Vague remediations: 'improve' is not a deliverable.
No tracking: the remediations die with the meeting notes.
lessons.try_it: Create the remediation tracker; review it at every IR meeting.

sections.heading: Zero Trust Principles
items: Never trust, always verify — a VPN authenticates the connection, then extends implicit trust to everything inside — the exact model zero trust rejects.
VPN limitations — a product with login MFA and then implicit trust is a VPN with better marketing.
Micro-perimeters — Micro-perimeters (host firewalls, service mesh policies, identity-aware proxies) enforce per-request decisions close to the resource.
Perimeter evolution — zero trust shrinks and multiplies the perimeter — down to individual resources and sessions — rather than eliminating it.
Common trap — zero trust means no perimeter at all.
Common trap — trust but verify: allow first, audit later.
Common trap — verify once at login, then trust the session indefinitely.
Common trap — assume breach means the SOC failed.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Identity & AD Defense
items: Phishing-resistant MFA — for privileged accounts, 'MFA' must mean phishing-resistant MFA; anything less is a speed bump, not a control.
Privileged access — defense is continuous hygiene (prune privileged groups, kill unconstrained delegation, remove stale admins) plus monitoring for the techniques (not just the paths).

Tiered admin model — credential theft (Mimikatz-style, token theft) harvests whatever is in memory on the compromised box — if that's a domain admin session, it's game over. Standing vendor admin accounts are a standing invitation — compromised vendor, compromised you.

Identity compromise response — full response: revoke everything, re-establish identity with strong MFA, and hunt the persistence mechanisms (mail forwarding rules, new devices, consented apps) before declaring it clean.
Session revocation — password reset alone leaves stolen session tokens and OAuth grants valid.
Common trap — just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, time-boxed rights, and full session logging; standing privilege is the risk.
Common trap — give every admin a second laptop with no restrictions.
Common trap — give them local admin on their laptops instead.
Common trap — let them browse from admin accounts.

sections.heading: Network Segmentation
items: Segmentation design — effective design groups by trust/function, puts policy enforcement (firewall/ACL) between segments, and — critically — tests that the policy actually denies. Discovery before enforcement is what makes segmentation survivable on legacy systems.

Enforcement — microsegmentation pushes enforcement to the workload (host firewalls, service-identity policies) so server-to-server traffic is authorized per policy, not trusted by subnet. Segmentation is enforcement, not labeling: VLANs without inter-VLAN access control…
East-west traffic — default-deny on unknown traffic breaks the business; allow-all teaches nothing.
OT segmentation — untested segmentation is a diagram, not a control. Re-test after changes — segmentation drifts as firewall rules accumulate exceptions.
Common trap — testing is the red team's job.
Common trap — segmentation doesn't apply to cloud.
Common trap — the DMZ is obsolete in zero trust.
Common trap — put the database in the DMZ for performance.

sections.heading: Cryptography
items: TLS everywhere — 'TLS everywhere' including east-west internal traffic is the zero-trust baseline; the performance argument died with modern hardware and TLS 1.3.

Internal encryption — in zero trust, workloads have identities too — IP addresses aren't identity. mTLS gives each service a cryptographic identity (certificate) verified on every connection, replacing 'it's on the internal network so it's fine.' Combined with short-lived certs…
Service identity — customer-managed keys (CMK/BYOK) add the separation: the provider can't decrypt without your key service, and you get the audit trail of key use.
Defense in depth crypto — explicit, documented classification turns crypto from a mandate into a risk-based design — and gives auditors the mapping they want.

Key management — and keys must live in an HSM/KMS — encryption with the key on the same disk is a locked safe with the combination taped to it. The zero-trust question is always 'who must I trust, and for what?' — key custody is trust made concrete.
Common trap — encryption is too slow for internal traffic.
Common trap — mTLS replaces the need for any authorization.
Common trap — encryption at rest is enough for everything.
Common trap — the cloud provider handles keys.

sections.heading: Allowlisting & Ringfencing
items: Allowlisting fails socially before it fails technically — if exceptions take weeks, users bypass the control entirely. Allowlisting answers 'may this run?'; ringfencing answers 'what may it touch?' A PDF reader has no legitimate need for PowerShell or internet access — ringfenced policies would have blocked both,…
Exception handling — a fast, risk-proportionate exception workflow (assess, scope, time-box, log, review) keeps the control credible.
Ringfencing — together they're defense in depth for the endpoint: allowlisting stops unknown code, ringfencing contains compromised known code.

Application containment — living-off-the-land attacks bypass application allowlists by using trusted interpreters for malicious scripts. Big-bang enforcement on 2,000 workstations is a self-inflicted outage — the real application baseline always differs from the inventory.
Common trap — exceptions prove allowlisting doesn't work.
Common trap — allowlist the antivirus itself and call it done.
Common trap — let managers approve their own exceptions permanently.
Common trap — only enforce on servers and skip workstations forever.

sections.heading: Red/Blue Operations
items: Purple teaming isn't a competition — it's collaborative adversary emulation where the red team shows its techniques in real time so the blue team can build detections.

Exercise goals — the exercise's ROI is measured in detections shipped and gaps closed — that's the continuous improvement loop that justifies the next exercise. 'Red won' with no detection improvement is a failed exercise; 'red succeeded, and we shipped six new detections a…

Rules of engagement — professional adversary emulation has: written authorization, scoped rules of engagement, safety constraints (no production destruction), SOC coordination (white-box, or controlled blind with safety rails), and an abort procedure.
Exercise safety — an exercise that ends at the report is entertainment. A program that repeats last year's exercise is measuring last year's threats.

Findings to detections — adversaries adapt, so emulation must too: rotate technique sets, emulate different actors' TTPs, and — critically — re-test old gaps, because detections regress as environments change.
Remediation loop — program metrics should track capability growth: technique coverage over time, detection/response times on realistic injects, and remediation velocity on findings.
Common trap — the red team 'winning' by owning the domain undetected.
Common trap — keeping the results secret so nobody looks bad.
Common trap — tell everyone the exact attack plan in advance.
Common trap — the blue team needs better products.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Zero Trust Principles: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
